item.title: The Legal System Is Taking Another Shot at Forcing Trump to Tell the Truth About January 6
Trump is making one more play to screw with the midterms
item.author: delivery_20261022061102.48033472.15032@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
California being the Trump administration’s target should come as no surprise. Outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom has been a constant critic of President Donald Trump. California is also the only Democrat-controlled state that successfully countered Trump’s mid-decade redistricting push, with voters there overwhelmingly passing a proposition to adopt new voting maps that could net up to five new Democrat-leaning House seats. The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to convince the Supreme Court to ban California from using its new maps because they were “tainted by an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.” Clearly still salty about that matter, among others, the administration seems to have been cooking up a new way to attack California.
Over the summer, Homeland Security sent California’s Secretary of State Shirley Weber a letter alleging that nearly 200,000 registered voters in California might be noncitizens (numerous secretaries of state received similar letters). But the letters included allegations alone, no evidence or data verifying DHS’s claims, which Weber said she flagged and asked to see, to no avail. Fast-forward to Oct. 13, when Weber, along with Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder and County Clerk Dean Logan received another letter, this time from the DOJ— before Election Day—asking them to review a list of over 20,000 individuals suspected of being noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot for the November election.
DOJ wanted both Weber and Logan to direct election officials across the state to “segregate” submitted ballots from voters whose citizenship could not “immediately be verified,” refrain from sending ballots to any more people on its list of 20,000 suspected noncitizens “until we confirm their citizenship status,” and “if a ballot for any individual on the list has been returned, instruct the appropriate elections official to not verify the signature and/or tabulate the ballot until citizenship can be determined.”
Weber and Logan were given approximately 48 hours to respond to the DOJ’s letter. And like clockwork, on Oct. 15 the DOJ filed a lawsuit asking a judge to issue a restraining order to prevent California election officials from processing ballots for any individual on its list of purported noncitizen voters. Never mind the fact that asking California to remove even a single name from its voter rolls at this point is a direct violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which established a 90-day “quiet period” before an election. This provision is meant to prevent states from doing exactly what the Trump administration is asking for: mass removals of voters too close to a federal election, which can cause confusion and prevent voters from fixing any registration issues with enough time left to cast their ballots.
Weber called this out in responding to the DOJ’s Oct. 13 letter. She cited the NVRA and the unlawful ask being put on her and election officials across California. “With less than three weeks before the election, you are demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide,” she said. Weber also went after DOJ’s list of 20,000 purported noncitizens registered to vote in California, reiterating that she requested the underlying data and methodology months ago in order to attempt to verify the federal government’s claims. As it stands, the DOJ's list effectively failed to “be of any investigative use.”
On Tuesday, a Los Angeles County election official responded in court to the DOJ’s lawsuit. She called the DOJ's demands potentially "catastrophic" and said they could end up halting all ballot counting, in person or by mail. She also revealed that election officials looked at a sample of 200 people on the federal government’s list and found that about 43 percent of them had a voter registration canceled, 71 percent had never actually cast a ballot, and nearly 40 percent indicated they U.S. citizens.
This would not be the first time the Trump administration’s alleged noncitizen voting lists were found to be inaccurate. Last month, the Trump administration admitted that a list of nearly 16,000 purported noncitizen voters it flagged for Nevada election officials was wholly inaccurate. After Nevada Deputy Attorney General Greg D. Ott attempted to verify DHS’s claims, he found that every single person on DHS’s list was actually a lawful U.S. citizen. And since Trump retook the presidency, his DOJ has sued 30 states and D.C. to get access to their unredacted voter rolls. Twenty-six of those lawsuits were dismissed by federal judges, half of whom were appointed by Republican presidents, including by Trump himself.
None of this matters to the Trump administration because its goal isn’t actually to weed out voter fraud, but to accomplish two things. First, these efforts seed doubt in America’s electoral process that could convince some voters to distrust the system to the point where they won’t bother casting a ballot. Second, these sham lawsuits give the administration a foothold in the courtroom in the event that a state’s election results are not satisfactory to Trump. Now, the DOJ and losing Republican candidates have a legal record to pull on to claim fraud and challenge state election results.
Rick Hasen, law professor at UCLA and director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project, described this approach in a recent post on his Election Law Blog. Though Hasen expects the DOJ's lawsuit against California “to go nowhere” in a court of law, he believes “this is a political document, potentially laying the groundwork for Trump to claim that the election results are illegitimate because California has not done enough to deal with noncitizen voting.”
To put a finer point on this, the DOJ this week announced a second lawsuit against 28 Californians for election crimes. They’re each being accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications—those applications ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship. A number of these folks, though, do not appear to , and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago, likely by accident. “Twenty-eight out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said. “It’s 0.0001% of all the registered voters, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Research backs this up, with one study finding that when noncitizen voting and registration does happen, it’s usually due to bureaucratic error and not intentional. For instance, just this year New Jersey revealed that its Motor Vehicle Commission improperly registered about 6,600 noncitizens to vote back in 2023, but fewer than 400 of them actually cast ballots between 2023 and 2024.
The Supreme Court has a hand in all of this, after it effectively emboldened the administration to pursue these types of lawsuits through an opinion issued just a month ago in DHS v. League of Women Voters. In a 6–3 decision, the justices have allowed the federal government to use an expanded federal database, known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, to identify noncitizen voting in states’ voter rolls.
What can be done now? Well, Americans are the only ones who carry the power of the vote, and right now they can control when they cast their ballots. As Joyce Vance, former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, emphasized, “this is the time to vote early.” It will be far more difficult for the Trump administration to challenge election results with ballots submitted weeks ahead of Election Day, especially when races have a large margin of victory. And that’s only possible with strong voter turnout.

item.title: The Flipbook of the Rings
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: For more than a year, marshalled by animator Andy Bailey, more than 1000 artists collaborated to create a hand-drawn, shot-for-shot, animated, flipbook version of Peter Jackson’s The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. The entire three hours. 120,000 individually drawn pages. A couple of months ago, they released the first 11 minutes:It’s pretty amazing. It doesn’t include the audio or music from the movie, but I bet you could mute the sound on this and simultaneously play the actual movie for the sound. Here’s an earlier sneak peek at some of the scenes:The first clip I claimed was a pretty iconic scene from the beginning of the movie. I chose to render it in pencil as it’s night time and I felt black and white would be more dramatic. As I worked through the frames, I did worry that the subtle variances in shading would make the clip look disjointed, but I think it adds a cool movement to the scene. There is that rough, quirky imperfection to hand drawing. You can see the final result with comparison below (digitized and compiled by Andy).I can’t wait to see the finished product — I hope they’re able to release it online.

item.title: New Developments in the Expanding “Wedgewood” Polling Scandal!
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I’m not sure where to start with this. The latest news is some mix of Webistics, Jukt Micronics and Animal House. But here goes. Yesterday we noted that a FiftyPlusOne investigation had led to the outing of “Wedgewood Polls” as a publisher of entirely fake polls. It’s still unclear the precise motives, but some political narrative setting aim and gaming betting markets seem like good bets. The details are wild. (But see the earlier post or FiftyPlusOne’s write-up for more.) Early this morning I woke to a short item in The Washington Post noting another pollster, SoCal Strategies, had straight up disappeared. By disappeared it meant that overnight its website, Substack and Twitter account had all vanished. In the earlier write-up of the investigation of Wedgewood, FiftyPlusOne had noted that one of the ways it had initially vetted Wedgewood was speaking to people at another polling firm where one or more of the Wedgewood guys had worked. I can’t remember if I’d already heard SoCal’s name come up in this story. But when I saw the Post item I immediately knew it had to be them. Yes, fake polls are a problem. But stuff like we’re seeing here is super rare. They had to be connected.

item.content:encoded: Here is one of those things we can see on the horizon and it will be important to be ready for. It will become especially important if Democrats take both the House and the Senate. It’s a given that even with only the House under Democratic control, we’re in for a period of pretty intense inter-branch conflict. Just how intense, whether Democrats will fight as much as their partisans demand … those things we can’t know. But this basic feature of the next Congress is pretty clear. item.title: Brian Evenson Will Mess With Your Head
item.author: Adam Fleming Petty
item.content:encoded: Brian Evenson’s first book, a story collection titled came out in 1994. It was not widely reviewed. The few notices the book did receive in the media ranged from the curious, to the baffled, to the outright disturbed. “In a capsule review, the nervously conceded that ‘there is a talent here,’ albeit, ‘an eldritch one,’” noted Ben Ehrenreich in an essay about Evenson’s work that appeared in One reviewer, though, an anonymous one, was unequivocal in their dismay over the book’s violent content, which included dismemberment, mutilation, insects placed in the mouths of corpses, and defenestration, among other indignities. “I feel like someone who has eaten something poisonous and is desperate to get rid of it,” wrote the nameless critic. This particular review would prove enormously consequential for Evenson’s career—indeed, for his life. It did not appear in a journal or a newspaper. It was not even published, technically. Rather, it was sent to Evenson’s employer, a university, triggering an inquiry that would lead to his dismissal. The nameless critic was a student at Brigham Young University, the flagship institution of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, located in Provo, Utah, where Evenson taught for the good reason that he was a devout Mormon, raised in the faith his whole life. The student wrote to the university out of concern that a violent, disturbing book like was not the sort of literary work that good Mormon professors should be pursuing. Over the course of the long and involved inquiry process, Evenson was presented with a choice. If he wished to continue working at BYU, he would have to stop writing books like that. If he didn’t stop, he would have to leave.

item.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: News today from Anthropic:We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP).I'm pleased to note I called this one last December, when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard":I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF, recently the new home of the MCP specification.Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to "Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body".

item.title: A Cool Night
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over atI have another soccer game to attend. This has been a parental duty for me and my wife ever since our son got into the sport sometime around the age of zero. You have kids, and you soon realize that the bulk of your time will be spent driving them places. As such, my wife and I have spent the past 17 years driving our son to soccer practice, soccer meetings, soccer games, and soccer team pizza parties. We’ve done this without malice, but the practice can’t help but turn a bit rote when you’ve been doing it for as long as we have.That’s been especially true during the boy’s senior year of high school. This year, he finally made the varsity team. No small accomplishment, but one that requires a great deal of his time and, by association, ours. Practices every day. Two games a week, some of them on the road, all of them extending relatively late into the evening. At one point, his team played a streak of half a dozen games that went to extra time; many of these were played in the rain, which I found extra rude. Some nights, he’s had to do his homework after coming back late from these games. Thus, the schedule is so demanding that the games, for any parent, can begin to feel like a bit of obligation.

item.title: Your Election Interference Fears Were 100% Justified
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: This Is Not a Drill … Repeat … NOT a DrillThe Trump administration has launched a full-blown attack on the midterm elections in California. It’s the very thing that everyone has been worrying that Trump would do for more than a year and yet … it doesn’t feel like the totality of what’s happening has really sunk in or embedded itself in the national political conversation as we sit here 12 days out from the end of voting.To recap for those just joining us, the Trump administration has used the false pretext of rampant noncitizen voting to:gin up criminal prosecutions nationwide against noncitizens for alleged voting-related crimes, with a special focus on California, where it rolled out a bunch of dubious new charges with high-profile arrests and official press conferences two weeks before the election;sue California to force it to segregate and mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters until it undertakes some new, uncertain, and open-ended investigation into whether the voters are citizens;send federal agents door-to-door looking for noncitizen voters in what is at best a fishing expedition and at worst a campaign to terrorize and instill fear in potential voters in minority communities.All of this happening — and I cannot emphasize it enough — universal mail-in voting is already underway in California.The various ways in which the Trump administration spent the past several months trying to monkey with the midterms — asserting unprecedented federal control over state-run federal elections, attempting to use the Postal Service to throttle mail-in ballot delivery, demanding access to voter rolls and individual voter information; marshaling federal databases in a purported effort to ferret out noncitizen voters; among other things — was merely a prelude to its open attack on the midterms now ongoing in California.The breadth and persistence of those earlier efforts by the administration has probably dulled the senses a bit and made it harder to distinguish what it happening now as a more serious and immediate threat to free and fair elections. The other complicating factor is that the fight to fend off the administration’s attack in California stretches from coast to coast, making it harder for reporters to cover it as a single unified story and for the public to grasp the various tendrils.There’s a major civil lawsuit underway in California and two separate important lawsuits in D.C. Plus the myriad criminal cases in California, which won’t be decided until after the election. At the same time, federal grand jury subpoenas are still outstanding that demand voter information from California election officials. And amidst all of that the Trump DOJ continues to actively threaten California election officials with prosecution if they don’t capitulate to administration demands.None of this is how the Justice Department behaved in the run up to past elections — quite the opposite.None of this is how to run an election.Drilling Down Into the DetailsI hope you’re still with me!Above is the high level view of the battlefield. If you only take away that broad impression, it’s all good.But of course, I want to dig down into all the specifics and give you updates on each front in this battle so you know exactly what you need to follow this closely. I’ll still try to keep it manageable in these next few items.More Threats From the Trump DOJI hadn’t zeroed in on this until yesterday, but in the litigation between the Trump DOJ and California, it emerged that acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, the No. 2 official, sent another letter last Friday containing an array of new threats against California election officials:The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime—and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful. Under 18 U.S.C. § 611(a), noncitizens are prohibited from voting in any election involving federal offices. Under 18 USC. § 2, anyone who aids, abets, ‘counsels, induces, or procures the commission of a federal offense is equally liable. If persons: knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors: to a federal crime.Administrative difficulty is not a defense to violating federal law or aiding or abetting a federal offense.The Department strongly urges the County and the SOS to reconsider their positions before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure.As California subsequently told a court, election officials are being asked to conduct the midterm elections under the threat of criminal prosecution from the federal government.DOJ Is Running Out of TimeIn the main case in California, where the Trump DOJ is suing to force California to segregate and not count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, both sides are seeking quick rulings.The Trump DOJ wants a TRO issued by noon PT .For now, the federal judge has set a hearing on the Trump DOJ’s TRO request for next Tuesday, Oct. 27. (The judge set this hearing before the Trump DOJ asked for a ruling by noon today.)With voting ending in 12 days, the timeframes are tight under every scenario. But they’re slightly tighter for the Trump DOJ, assuming it wants to get this case to the Supreme Court in an emergency posture before Election Day, a fair assumption.Meanwhile, in D.C. Federal Court …U.S. District Judge James Boasberg is overseeing two separate but related cases that are challenging more broadly aspects of the Trump administration’s attack on the midterm elections. As of yesterday, Judge Boasberg put one of those cases on an expedited pre-election timeline similar to the California case. The other case, just filed on Tuesday, isn’t moving as quickly yet, but it may.I’m sparing you details on these cases until they ripen a bit more.Judge Halts DHS Voter Fraud OpsIn yet another case, a federal judge in California blocked DHS from carrying out field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The order is to remain in place until the polls close on Nov. 3.The judge was most concerned with U.S. citizens getting swept up in and being intimidated by the DHS field ops, so she blocked ops when they are “likely to involve” people who DHS agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.”That leaves some wiggle room for DHS to exploit.The judge’s ruling came the same day that CBS News reported that armed and uniformed DHS agents have have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status, in an operation that ramped up beginning in September.“[T]he public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed Defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens,” U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote.While the California battlefront is the most urgent and pressing threat to the midterms, I would still assess as low the Trump administration’s chances of ultimately prevailing in court. But that doesn’t mean it can’t win. And even more importantly, the fight itself is part of the point and is doing real damage right now by actually interfering in an ongoing election.Third Country Removal UpdateUpdates on a couple of the most egregious third country removals that I’ve mentioned over the last couple of months:: A federal judge in California has confirmed that a wrongfully deported Nigerian national is back in the United States after she ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. Etinosa Osahon — who was legally barred from being deported to Nigeria because he had already been tortured twice there and was at risk of future torture — was wrongfully deported in May to Ghana, which promptly attempted to transfer him to Nigeria. He refused to continue on the overland journey and was dumped en route in Togo, where he had remained in hiding.: A federal judge in Arizona who ordered the Trump administration on Oct. 6 to facilitate the return of an Egyptian national who had been deported to Equatorial Guinea ratcheted up the pressure on the administration to act more quickly to abide by his original order. The new order comes after Gillian Brockell reported that an ICE deportation flight was scheduled to arrive in Equatorial Guinea today but still not retrieve Ahmed Soliman, whose health is reportedly rapidly deteriorating.The Retribution: Free Press EditionIn a retaliatory move, the Trump White House removed Andrew Feinberg, the reporter whom it derided earlier this week as a “Mongoloid moron,” from the out-of-town print pool for President Trump’s trip to Iowa today.In an extraordinary letter, a White House lawyer demanded that Politico retract a series of palace intrigue stories on Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, concluding his letter with this not-at-all-veiled retaliatory threat:I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives. Failure to do so or otherwise respond justifying Politico’s publications within 48 hours will prompt an immediate review of Politico’s relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies.Hegseth Broke Eisenhower’s GlobeThe WaPo, with a metaphor for our time: Hegseth wanted Eisenhower’s globe for his office. His staff broke it.

item.title: Basketball Game Interrupts Shit-Talk Session Between Luka Doncic And Yaxel Lendeborg
item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: For months, I've seen Michigan basketball fans chortle ominously about the big personality of Yaxel Lendeborg, the super-senior who led the Wolverines' 2026 national championship run then sidled over to the NBA draft, where he was selected at No. 11 by the Golden State Warriors. They'd murmur something about him being blunt, being goofy, the world isn't ready for him, etc. Sure.I knew the backstory: Born to parents who had both played basketball for the Dominican Republic's national teams, Lendeborg barely participated in organized basketball for most of his schooling because he couldn't keep his grades up, preferring instead to play video games all day, and had no intention to play college ball until pushed by his mom to play in a showcase for Dominican players at the end of high school. His highlights there won him the last scholarship slot at Arizona Western College, and after a cumulative six seasons of college hoops, a first-round NBA draft selection, a Summer League MVP, and a strong preseason, he started at power forward in his NBA debut on Wednesday. A remarkable sequence of events.The Warriors targeted 24-year-old Lendeborg rather than taking a younger prospect, presumably because they wanted a fresh-out-of-the-box starter to retain a competitive team around Steph Curry. It's a noble thought, but at least one game in, with Jimmy Butler still months away from a return after ACL repair, and Kristaps Porzingis reportedly considering retirement due to chronic illness, the Warriors look dismal. While they were getting shredded by the Los Angeles Lakers, 127-105, Lendeborg exchanged lots of animated words and gestures with inveterate shit-talker Luka Doncic. Just before the halftime buzzer, Doncic banked in a half-court shot over Lendeborg, and the two resumed barking at each other.

item.title: It’s Hard To Be A Rich Radical
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: , a column where I share the music and musical topics I’ve been fixated on recently.What could compel someone to spend four hours on a YouTube essay mostly about the rapper Killer Mike, a B-tier Dungeon Family affiliate who parlayed success as one half of Run The Jewels to become a B-tier rap A-lister? In truth, it is no worse than sitting through six hours of self-assigned Super Bowl performer Jay-Z and Rick Rubin yap about rap and also therapy. Or watching a three-hour documentary on disgraced Silicon Valley fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in a hilariously, extremely sold-out theater. Or watching four hours of Nick Saban coaching propaganda. Or one hour of an ESPN soft-focus profile of Ben Simmons that tries to sidestep the question of Simmons’ work ethic. I watch a lot of nonsense, I guess it’s safe to say—and people are apparently greatly long-winded.Maybe a better question is: Who would actually be compelled to a four-hour YouTube video on Killer Mike? For that answer, we’d have to get into who FD Signifier and Jared A. Ball are, and the importance of the latter’s book, . Then we would have to talk about black leftist politics and anticapitalist critique and how exactly we got to a point where a bunch of people think Killer Mike is at war with black activist streamers and content creators, and shooting at them in random freestyles.

item.title: Vivek Ramaswamy Is Going After The Abusive Parent Vote
item.author: David Roth
item.content:encoded: This is not to discredit the existence of some underlying tactical or strategic calculations, and it is absolutely not extending credit to the shockingly vile creatures doing it, but when you see a reactionary candidate being disgusting, it is safe to assume that they are doing it because they really believe in it. The decade and change in which Donald Trump has been the main character in American public life has been a notably bad one for metaphor and subtext, among other things, but it has been a notably revealing one where some fundamental national political impulses are concerned. Trump himself is too dim and too brazen for that game's familiar euphemisms, and his inability or unwillingness to promise to deliver harm in the usual coded language was central to his political appeal. It was also novel enough to convince some people that he was interested in doing something other than inflicting that pain.This was true for partisans who thrilled at hearing him make explicit the implicit conservative value of hurting the most vulnerable people, and also to a significant faction of people without any other real values who mistook the brutal liberties that Trump has always taken for himself for ones that they would be able to enjoy themselves by supporting him. There is no other way to say it: Donald Trump these people. He inspired them to be their worst and smallest and cruelest selves, but inspiration is a value-neutral thing. This is to say that he inspired those people to be more like him, and to live as he lives—in the indulgent certainty that even their puniest comfort or fleeting amusement or flash of childish anger was more important than anything or anyone else in the world, and then to behave accordingly. Many of these people surely had suspected as much already and moved through the world as if it were true; the carnage and stupid suffering that all that heedless, headlong motion produces is everywhere you look. Some of these people, inevitably, were going to run for political office.People like that will always be a danger to everyone around them, but it's at this point that they truly become everyone's problem. There is a world in which Vivek Ramaswamy is just one of the many millions of Americans—please do not think about how many there are, how many you have met and will someday meet—who just are , and move through their days with what even a layperson could diagnose as "walking malignant narcissism." But that alternate-universe Ramaswamy would be contained within some grim gated community and grim gated personal and business relationships; his capacity to do the damage such a person would invariably do would be limited to those unfortunate enough to wind up in his path. That Ramaswamy would also be an extremely odious man, a curdled being driven entirely by resentment and appetite. But very few people would ever know his name. That's the best-case scenario.

item.title: Aaron Sorkin Wants To Pretend The Good Guys Won
item.author: Imran Zaidi
item.content:encoded: In 2000, midway through the first season of , Aaron Sorkin started posting on a discussion forum on the site Television Without Pity as “Benjamin,” his middle name. Specifically, he posted on the forum dedicated to discussing . “Benjamin” was met with some initial skepticism, but after proving to their satisfaction that he really was the show’s creator, his interactions with fans were warm. They fawned over him, and he thanked them for watching. Things took a turn in 2001 when posters commented on Sorkin’s unseemly hogging of the mic in an acceptance speech for an Emmy he won with a co-writer, Rick Cleveland. The incident snowballed into full-fledged forum drama, with Sorkin and Cleveland trading lengthy, bitter replies; Sorkin eventually admitted he was wrong, apologized, and stopped posting. Later, when the site’s recaps took a more critical turn, he reappeared, angry and defensive, asking why the recapper was even bothering to watch the show and write about it if she didn’t like it. The site’s founder responded that the recapper was doing this because it was her job and they paid her. This was Sorkin’s first dance with the internet, and it seems to have left a mark. An entire storyline in a third-season episode is dedicated to White House deputy chief of staff Josh Lyman discovering a Josh Lyman fan forum and accidentally running afoul of its hostile, pajama-clad users. The forum’s moderator, who polices infractions like posting in the wrong thread or writing in all caps, is described by Josh as “a dictatorial leader who I’m sure wears a muumuu and chain-smokes Parliaments.” Sorkin’s next TV show, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip, careened between goofy comedy and somber drama as it struggled and ultimately failed to find its footing, but a consistent thread was the corrosive influence of the internet, manifested in everything from unscrupulous gossip bloggers to foreign terrorists posting hostage videos on YouTube. was similarly erratic in tone while even more laser-focused on the harm that the likes of Gawker and Twitter were causing to journalism, politics, and our very souls. In its unapologetically pro-elite credentialism, its score-settling attitude toward women, and its often deranged determination to offer Frank Capra-style uplift no matter the circumstances, the show remains the purest distillation of Sorkin’s fixations.In 2010, when was released, the general public largely still trusted the tech industry. The iPhone felt futuristic. Facebook was still kind of cool. Today, depicting Silicon Valley as a malign force is cliché; 16 years ago, it was subversive. The alchemy of Sorkin’s collaboration with David Fincher—a non-obvious director for a quippy, dense script—resulted in a perfectly calibrated dark comedy warning us about the future of human interaction and the people bringing it into being. In the decade that followed, reality caught up to the film’s bleak outlook. The preoccupations that had once marked Sorkin as an aggrieved and out-of-touch Luddite now made him look improbably prescient. It makes sense that he would feel the urge to take a victory lap.

item.title: The 'best Mexican restaurant in the world' is in SF. It only cost me $500.
item.content:encoded: There is exactly one three-starred Michelin-rated Mexican restaurant in the world, and somewhat rudely, it’s not in Mexico. It’s Californios, a $450 prix fixe gastronomic temple tucked away on 11th Street in the SoMa neighborhood of San Francisco. You already know this kind of restaurant simply from the price point (which rose $50 since my visit, from $325 to $375 before tax/tip/drinks), and from the fact that it got the notice of the fabled Michelin judges this year, who went so far as to declare it the best Mexican restaurant in the world. Is this the kind of place custom made for its patrons to boast about having dined there? Of course. Does the 12-course tasting menu include fantasy novel ingredients such as “chickweed”? You bet it does. Do certain dishes come with tweezers? Bitch, you KNOW there are gonna be some tweezers coming your way. As long as epicureanism exists, there will always be establishments like this one: ones that are equal parts thrilling, exhausting and ultra-expensive.But, knowing what you and I know about the post-COVID world, about the darker side of Michelin-starred kitchens, and about America’s ever-worsening income gap, is the kind of restaurant that dollops caviar onto multiple courses still ? That’s where I come in. Because tonight, I’ll be dining at Californios for the very first time …Article continues below this adI’m not lying when I tell you this restaurant is tucked away. As with so many restaurants of its caliber, Californios, open since 2015, hangs no shingle by its entrance. You have to know it’s there to it’s there, and even then, you can still miss it. I know because I just walked right by Californios’ front door without realizing it, then had to double back as I stared at the pin on Google Maps, then double back again when I walked right by it a second time. This is fine dining as speakeasy: No walk-ins allowed, and the only way in is by securing a reservation months in advance. Again, you and I know this kind of place.Then I saunter through the main entrance and am instantly transported. I’m standing inside a stone courtyard dotted with luxe wicker patio furniture and potted palm trees. Every muscle in my body slackens. A few steps farther, and now I’m inside a flawlessly lit dining room with walls painted a deep, rich blue and adorned with vibrant paintings that I’d probably pay a separate entrance fee just to stare at. I wish I lived here.Article continues below this adThe host escorts me to my table, and I feel a touch sad to be dining alone. This is the kind of place you take her after she’s said yes, you know what I mean? Californios offers romantic ambience in endless abundance. Now I miss my wife. I better stuff myself with 900 pounds of quail mole and black cod tacos to help dull the heartache.Then I get the menu, and it looks exactly like a wedding program. There’s even a tasteful photograph of a flower affixed to the cover. I half expect to open it and see that my meal will begin with a procession to Vivaldi, followed by a reading from Corinthians. There’s also an autographed welcome card on the table addressed to a “Brodie,” which is not my name but the name of the person who booked my reservation. My server apologizes and promises to get me a new envelope with my actual name on it. I tell them it’s OK. On this night, I’d rather be Brodie. Makes me feel stealthy.That’s enough prelude. Let’s get to the good stuff, shall we? My evening begins with a flight of aguas frescas: strawberry hibiscus soda, canary melon horchata, and guava/kiwi soda. I also order a separate, a la carte mocktail: a coca noza, Mexican Coke with cherry. All of it is delicious. I love fancy sodas. My appetite has now been sufficiently whetted. I could eat a whole bull right now.Article continues below this adI’ll have to settle for a series of arty small plates instead. As with many other high-end omakase restaurants, dinner at Californios is an overextended affair in which you, the diner, must endure an hourslong procession of courses, each of which includes a little guest lecture from your server before you feel allowed to partake. That waiting can prove a bit torturous, but the tease is part of the burlesque. So I can’t help but groan with pleasure when I finally get to take my first bite: an Anasazi bean sope, or beancake, topped with caviar. I’m a sucker for caviar, and pairing it with this cake, which has been stuffed with a gigante bean mousse, is exactly the stroke of genius I’d expect from chef-owner Val Cantu, who’s originally from Texas and mastered the craft of Mexican cooking during a stint working at Mexico City’s Pujol. I hear another diner say, “This tastes like a memory,” which was surely Cantu’s goal. In this mission, he is fabulously successful. This is food that makes you think, and that makes you to think.But all that thinking tends to make one hungry. Here comes more modestly sized appetizers — a bluefin tuna tostada that’s been topped with serrano coins and finishes hot on the palate. It’s a slow burn that I hope lingers a good long while. Then comes a single Dungeness crab flauta. I’m a sucker for flautas, too. This is Mexican food all right: instantly recognizable and yet new all at the same time. I want more.Article continues below this adI get it. While sucking down the rest of my coca noza, I’m greeted with a disc of lobster ceviche sitting in a pool of “spicy water,” the latter of which is far tastier than its name implies. The server tells me that I’m free to slurp this aguachile, and I happily take him up on the entreaty. Now here’s abalone on the shell, which I take down in seconds. Every bite here only makes me hungry for more. I suspect that, even after all of these bravura small bites, the Californios kitchen is holding back on the big flavors for the later courses. My patience, admittedly, is wearing a touch thin. The quail mole and rib-eye tacos are still many courses away, and I’m wanting to go to there.When on my table what should appear but a grilled banana flan topped with serrano ham, date jus, translucently thin plantain chips and, natch, more caviar. I have never tasted anything like this, and likely never will again. In the pre-COVID times, experiential dining like this was revered to the point of absurdity. It feels a bit more crass to enjoy it in a broken 2026 America. But man, eat that flan and tell me if it’s a moral abdication or not. I’m sorry that not everyone gets to try this, but I’m not sorry that get to.After I lay waste to that savory flan, my server tells me, “Now we’re moving on to tacos.” F—k yeah, we are.Article continues below this adAnother showstopper follows: a single fish taco. But this is no ordinary fish taco. Cantu and his staff have battered a rectangle of black cod (aka sable, aka butterfish), placed it atop a sourdough tortilla, and then topped the fish with a corn smut crema and multi-pepper salsa. Frying black cod is a very evil and awesome thing to do. This is the best fish taco I’ve ever eaten, in part because of the aforementioned cod,but also thanks to the sourdough tortilla. I hope sourdough tortillas make it off the runway and down into the retail dining sector sooner rather than later.It has taken literal hours for me to get through these opening acts, and my back is a touch sore. I get back up to enjoy the courtyard, plus a bathroom that features a toilet with a seat that opens and closes automatically. Makes me feel like a heavy hitter.Article continues below this ad the kitchen brings out the big guns. First up is the aforementioned quail mole, which is presented so artfully that I want to hang it on the dining room wall: a diamond-shaped piece of quail breast covered in a mole that surely contains 936 separate ingredients and required 47 hours to make. The mole coats the breast entirely, leaving only a clean matte finish that reflects the light fixtures hanging overhead. To one side of that plate is the leg quarter of that same quail smoked, its lower portion wrapped in twine for easy gripping. To the other side, a bowl of fresh tortillas (not sourdough) crusted in sesame seeds. At certain points during this meal, I kept expecting a burrito to arrive, because I am long conditioned for a specific kind of Mexican food, which, to be clear, kicks major ass. At other points, I’ve wondered if I’d be left so hungry by all these small plates that I would have to go purchase said burrito at another restaurant after dinner was over. The mole makes all of those cravings and worries disappear. I am being both blown away and sated all in one go.Ah, but we’re not done yet. Because after the mole comes a final taco, this one stuffed with ribbons of sliced rib-eye that are so tender, they never catch on my teeth. Even better, the kitchen has paired this steak taco with a glass of beet juice (as part of the N/A drink pairings I ordered to go with my tasting menu, at a supplemental cost of $95, now $125) that’s so deep in color and texture that it behaves like red wine. As someone who no longer drinks alcohol and has found all dealcoholized red wines to be rotgut, I’m downright grateful for this glass of beet juice to go with my final taco. I don’t even normally like beets, man. Then again, I am not me tonight. I am Brodie. Brodie will f—k up some beet juice.Now for dessert. Do they crumb your table before serving you dessert here? You needn’t ask. The main dessert is a chocolate alegría — a kind of traditional Mexican candy — topped with strawberries, lightly toasted amaranth and solidified honey bits. Its satellite desserts include a blueberry empanada and a scoop of almond ice cream, which, when eaten in tandem, is the kind of dessert I would like to eat every night until I’m dead. They spoil you with desserts at Californios, right down to the candied mandarin segments that come with my check. It’s late now, far too late, but I, the mysterious Brodie, will be heading back to my hotel room more than satisfied.Article continues below this adIf not conflicted. Again, this is an extremely pricey restaurant. An one. So while I had myself a grand ol’ time at Californios, even without a proper date sitting across from me, I’m still left to wonder if this sort of restaurant can exist in the 21st century, and if it even should. Does the world still need restaurants where the starting price is about the same as a fancy hotel room, where every course comes with its own special set of utensils, and where any question you ask about your food will get you a crisp paragraph in reply? Isn’t this all a bit ostentatious? Do we really want a place like this to still have cultural purchase?After thinking about it, my answer remains an unequivocal yes. Yes, sitting for an hourslong dinner is kind of an ordeal, and the money spent by customers here would be better spent on helping the destitute, and maybe not every restaurant should have a menu that literally includes pages’ worth of end credits. Would I have preferred to eat all of Californios’ dishes from an a la carte menu, over successive (and much more brief) visits? Of course. But then Cantu’s restaurant might not have gotten quite as much notice from Michelin, which still represents the vanguard of the fine dining establishment. It may not have been recognized as three-star runway food. Article continues below this adAnd runway food, of the highest Michelin rating, still needs to exist for the same reason that all high art needs to exist. The world, no matter what condition it’s in, will always need people who feverishly labor to give others something they’ve never experienced before; people who act as credible tastemakers in the greater culture for the coming years, if not decades. That’s especially true in the case of Californios, because it has given Mexican food long-overdue representation in the highest stratosphere of culinary gatekeeping. It’s the first three-star Mexican restaurant in the world, but it will not be the last.

item.title: Preznit Fuckwit knows he’s losing his mind, and it’s scaring him shitless
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Dear Leader’s brain has gone .You know it, and I know it.The worthless scribblers of the corporate-controlled press know it, too, though they try like hell to dance around the subject.The GOP establishment — lickspittles and bottom-feeders like Holy Mike Johnson and John Thune — they know it, too. But their political futures depend on pretending it’s not happening.Here’s the real question, though — does Dear Leader understand just how cognitively collapsed he is? Consider this: when Lord Shitticus, lost in a thick haze of dementia, wanders past the open door of his waiting limo, as he did the other night, and then snaps back to reality to find himself in the middle of a field, surrounded his panicked security contingent — the deteriorating old dumbfuck has to realize that something is seriously wrong, doesn’t he?“But my wife, uh— said to me— I mimicked Sleepy Joe walking off the stage, you know, I had a wall behind me in that case, and I walked into the wall. You know, walked around aimlessly. Had no idea. And— I thought it was— the place was cracking up, right? And then I came back and I finished my speech, and I said, ‘baby, how good was that tonight? Was that the best? No one can do it like me, baby. You see that crowd?’ And she said, ‘what happened to you? Are you okay?’ I said, ‘what do you mean?’ ‘They had you walking around the stage, hitting the wall. Are you okay, darling?’”Oh look, it’s a — the first-lady-themed version of a Whenever Donny recounts a tale wherein the Slovenian rent-a-wife who despises him and recoils at his touch calls him ‘darling’ — that’s when you know it’s a big ball of No, Melania did not come up to Donny after his speech, big, strong, teary-eyed like few thought possible, and go, ‘Donal! Donal! Vat wrong vit you oh my darlink Donal?’Let’s get real. Mel doesn’t live with Donny. She doesn’t travel with him. If anyone come up to Donny and express concern after a speech, it would have been Diaper Nurse Natty. But what you really have to love is how Donny blames his inability find his way off the stage on Joe Biden. Sleepy Joe made me do it!“I’d say 90% of the reason I took the governor— EUHHHP.”Fuck me, what even was that sound? Did Donny just cough up a hairball? Donny’s losing the ability to make his rancid anus-mouth function properly. But please, Donny, tell us one more time now you were just imitating Joe Biden. That’s such a cool story.“I settled all these wars, and— they gave the— wonderful PEACE prize, right? Does anyone know the name of that peace prize? The peace prize. They gave the Pulitzer Prize to— a YOUNG LADY. I think she’s eighty years old. A young lady who— nobody ever heard of.”It’s the Nobel Peace Prize, you sub-sentient suppurating pustule. How do you fuck that up? There is no Pulitzer Peace Prize. The Pulitzer committee doesn’t dole out prizes for peacefully-written sentences. Did Joe Biden’s autopen make you say that?Donny’s barely coherent — and I’m being generous when I say ‘barely.’ He now speaks in that weird, halting syntax, full of odd pauses and nonsensically emphasized words. Take a gander at the crowed of numbskulls behind Dear Leader. They’re completely checked out. They didn’t sign up for this. They came to be entertained, but now they’re just confused.Look at this bro behind Donny. He so fucking bored that he can’t stop yawning. All he can think is ‘when will this shit be over?’ Yeah, that’s one motivated Republican voter, right there.Look, I understand that Donny to be holding these hate-rallies, night after night, right up to the midterms. But he can’t hack it any more. Letting him do this to himself is just elder abuse at this point. He should be back at the White House, with the diaper nurse spoon-feeding him from a pudding cup.President Trump’s approval rating hit a new low just weeks before the midterm elections, driven by broad disapproval of his handling of the economy, the war in Iran and high gas prices, according to a new poll from The New York Times and Siena University. Fox News: “There’s a potential President Trump visit to Minnesota. Would that help or hurt you?”Michele Tafoya: “Listen, uh, I don’t know anything about his schedule. I'm certainly not in charge of his schedule.” She then goes on to change the subject — but the Fox bobblehead is having none of it.Fox: “But would he help your case?”Tafoya: “Look, again, I think for some it might, and for some it might not.” Look at that — when asked to commit to a straightforward answer — yes or no — Brave Sir Michele runs away, away. In any other election cycle, having the sitting president come to personally campaign for you would be a boon — but not in 2026. Donny is a toxic waste dump. He’s a superfund cleanup site.Let’s move from 2026 to 2028, because here’s another question for you: who do you see as the GOP front-runner for prez? Oh sure, Couchfuck McGee, Piss-Drunk Pete, and Liddle Marco Big-Shoes all want to president, but let’s face it — none of those clowns has a snowball’s chance. They’re all repellent.Reporter: “Mr. President, since we have the vice president here, the vice president said in an interview yesterday, that he thought you would endorse him if he does decide to run in 2028. Since we’re here, could you tell us—”Donny: “Well, I’ll tell you. There’s— he’s a very talented person and he’s a good person, but we’ve literally— I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it. Who would believe that.”How humiliating for Couchfuck McGee. All he can do is stand behind Dear Leader, with a fake smile plastered on his stupid face, and croak out an insincereEven his lord and master knows he’s a fucking loser.Here’s the thing: the GOP has no rising young stars. They have no future. Donny’s made sure of that, by running anyone with half a brain right out of the party. It’s shitwits and fucksticks all the way down. Reporter: “There was a report in Politico the other day that FEMA is telling states to begin to prepare to handle disasters on their own. Do you have reaction to this?”Jon Ossoff: “So the Trump administration is telling folks across the country to prepare to fend for themselves if a natural disaster hits while taxpayer dollars are sent to back Don Jr and Eric's mining interest in Kazakhstan?”As I never tire of saying, Jon Ossoff is so good at this. No matter what the subject, he’ll masterfully tie it to the high crimes and corruption of Donny and his felonious family.Ask him what time it is, and he’ll be all, ‘it’s Donny is a thieving bastard o’clock.’I’m liking our chances in 2026 — and I’m liking our chances in 2028.And I’m liking the Daily Claudia, so let’s have one.here’s a triptych from September 12, 2024, taken at a harbor-side cafe whose name I’ve forgotten, in Wickford, Rhode Island.Have a great Thursday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Ottawa Vs. Brady Tkachuk Was Fantastic Theater
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: There's a type of hate that's easy to love. It's the hate a downtrodden fanbase feels for a homegrown star who forced his way out, to a better or at least more glamorous situation. This hate is full and rich and multifaceted. It contains all the frustrations of decades of losing, of free agents spurning their team as a destination, of being a punchline for the rest of the league. It contains envy and resentment toward the idea that someone could just choose not to live or die with the fortunes of that benighted franchise. It contains disappointment in that departed star, for getting their hopes up and leaving them dangling. It contains a heart-tugging exasperation that gets deep into sports' very real ability to encapsulate the human condition: it says. Not since Long Island "welcomed" back John Tavares has there been a night of hockey hate like Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa on Wednesday. He may be Keith Tkachuk's garbage son, but for eight years he was Ottawa's garbage son, too, dammit. Ottawa's easy to root for from afar. They've dealt with more shit than any fanbase should be expected to. They weathered an evil and stupid owner, and threats of relocation. They've been the butt of the joke on the ice, failing to win a playoff series in the last decade and reaching one Final in their entire existence. Everyone dumps on their town, even, accidentally, their own mayor. Players don't want to live there. If they are to have their very own superstar, they have to make one. For the Senators' drawn-out trek into and then gradually out of the wilderness, that was Brady Tkachuk.Tkachuk makes a great bad guy. He already has the bearing and showmanship of a pro-wrestling heel, and the way he forced his way to Florida was genuinely villainous: quietly, on the mythical Team USA group chat, and publicly, on his podcast with his father and brother. (Tampering is an unenforceable rule, but it's to not even try to pretend to follow it.) He's an avatar for the U.S.'s aggressive geopolitical little-brothering of Canada. He's unlikable as a person and infuriating as an opposing player. He is very fun to boo, and he is of the temperament to enjoy being booed.

item.title: The Dream Are Making Bully Ball Literal
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: There's a sequence from the first quarter of Game 3 of the WNBA Finals, in which the Atlanta Dream walloped the Golden State Valkyries by a score of 97-71, that would still be grinding my gears if I were a Valks fan. Angel Reese, fresh off her Game 2 masterpiece, started Game 3 aggressively, going right to the rim. She scored the first two points of the game on a nifty duck-in, and then tried to drive on Kiah Stokes on two straight possessions. Stokes blocked her both times, and then blocked a Jordin Canada layup. And then, with just over five minutes left in the quarter, Stokes was subbed out of the game.One of the most noticeable subplots of these Finals is what Reese is able to do when Stokes is and is not matched up with her. When defended by Stokes, she has sometimes struggled to reliably get off clean shots; against every other big on the Valks' roster, she has enjoyed a feast of layups and fouls. Things were no different on Wednesday night: As soon as Aminata Gueye subbed in for Stokes in the first quarter, Reese went straight at her for a bucket and a foul. When Stokes was subbed out again with 7:23 left in the second quarter, Reese got right back to work by hitting a three in Gueye's face and then bumping her out of the way for another layup.The Valkyries and Dream are stylistically similar in a number of meaningful ways, but one area where they diverge is their depth. Golden State has ridden its 10-player rotation to the Finals by believing in every player's ability to contribute, and by prioritizing meaningful amounts of in-game rest for the starters. The Dream, meanwhile, are happy to share minutes among just seven players. A deep roster full of talented players is the kind of thing that can help carry a team through the regular season and a long playoff run, but a dogmatic commitment to using a big rotation can make it harder to navigate that other all-important principle of playoff basketball: matchups.

item.title: Bizarre Cephalopod Reproduction
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Warning: this video contains marine animal sex and plenty of jokes about it. After all, it's a True Facts video from Ze Frank. He offers classroom-friendly version of his videos, but admits that this one might be difficult to translate. We've already been through the argument over the plural of octopus many times, but what about cuttlefish? If there are two, is it cuttlefishes or cuttlefish? It's important because it takes two cuttlefish to make babies. But they don't quite cuttle the way you'd expect. For one thing, cephalopod sperm is delivered in biological packages that are about as complex as a space ship to overcome the effects of living underwater. The different species shown here use a variety of methods to deliver them. Male octopi use an arm, which might even detach. Squids, cuttlefish, and octopi know what they're doing, although it looks all wrong to us. The result is eggs laid and a new generation hatched, even if it kills a parent.

item.title: Ken Paxton says he’ll never quit fighting. Neither will we.
item.author: 1axbuan7swno5tsx5nusjsu2yhfvuxema5i2eb@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: On Jan. 6, 2021, hours before the insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, a man addressed a crowd of angry Trump supporters near the White House.“If you look at Georgia, they capitulated, they consented. We kept fighting in Texas,” he said. He closed with a promise: “We will not quit fighting.”That man, Ken Paxton, has been terrorizing Texas for years, first as a member of the state Legislature and then as the state’s attorney general. Now, as he closes out his campaign for the U.S. Senate, he wants to take his reign of terror nationwide.Paxton is one of the country’s most outspoken and active election deniers, and it’s not hard to imagine how disastrous he would be as a senator. Just look at his record.Like Donald Trump, Paxton does not accept election results he doesn’t like. And like Trump, he believes in wielding power by weaponizing government.As Texas attorney general, he sprang into action to try to overturn the 2020 presidential election. He even bragged about the failed attempt in his Jan. 6 speech:“We sued four states over the ballot fraud and not following the Constitution, not following state law, and we took it directly to the Supreme Court. And they should have heard our case.”Let me be clear: In no world should the Supreme Court have heard Paxton’s case.

item.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Hermanos Gutiérrez, Ecuadorian-Swiss guitarists Alejandro and Estevan. We recommended them in 2024 and 2023. Estevan started playing guitar in elementary school, focusing on milonga (Argentinian folk) and classical; later on, Alejandro taught himself guitar. The brothers started playing together regularly after a spontaneous jam session at Alejandro’s apartment. Hermanos Gutiérrez formed on a trip to the American southwest, specifically the Mojave Desert and Death Valley; “the desert is where our music was born,” Estevan told Premier Guitar. Their new record, , came out in September. The idea for the record occurred to the brothers upon seeing a 1973 photo of their dad in Machu Picchu; throughout, Estevan plays the nylon guitar his father gave him at eight years old. The cinematic and evocative tracks are odes to the Andean mountain landscape. We’re also revisiting their 2024 record, , which has more of a psychedelic sound, as the title suggests. Both records were produced by Dan Auerbach of the Black Keys.

item.title: Empire Records: The Beautiful Genius of a Movie That Understood Being Young
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: ** I’m not going to bury the lead here. Youtube Movies currently has Empire Records available to stream for free. So here it is, if you don’t want to read the article I spent an hour writing, have at it **Now if you actually wanna read it……..Some movies capture a moment in time so perfectly that they become more than entertainment. They become time capsules, preserving the music, fashion, attitudes, anxieties, and absurd little details of a generation. is one of those movies. Released in 1995, it arrived with an unassuming story about a group of record store employees trying to save their workplace, but beneath its modest premise was something much more meaningful: a celebration of individuality, friendship, music, and the terrifying, exhilarating experience of figuring out who you are.At the box office, didn’t exactly set the world on fire. Critics were largely unimpressed, and the movie initially struggled to find an audience. Yet over the years, it developed a devoted following, particularly among people who recognized themselves in its collection of outsiders, misfits, music obsessives, and young adults who hadn’t quite figured out what they wanted from life.Its enduring appeal isn’t an accident. The genius of lies in its understanding that growing up rarely happens through grand revelations. Sometimes it happens during an awful shift at work, an argument with a friend, a terrible decision made at two in the morning, or a conversation with someone who understands you better than you understand yourself.And sometimes, it happens in a record store.A Simple Story With Something Bigger at Its HeartThe premise of is deceptively straightforward. The employees of an independent record store discover that their beloved workplace is in danger of being absorbed into a corporate chain. Over the course of a chaotic day, they navigate personal problems, romantic entanglements, musical ambitions, financial disasters, and the usual assortment of teenage catastrophes.On paper, this sounds like the foundation for a conventional workplace comedy. In practice, the record store becomes a miniature world where each character represents a different struggle with identity, insecurity, ambition, or belonging.The store isn’t merely where the characters work. It’s where they spend their lives, where they find their friends, and where they feel most comfortable being themselves. It provides a refuge from parents, school, social expectations, and the increasingly complicated business of becoming an adult.That distinction matters. For many young people, a first job is simply a way to earn money. But occasionally, a workplace becomes a community. The people behind the counter become your friends. The customers become familiar faces. The music playing through the speakers becomes the soundtrack to an entire chapter of your life. understands that emotional connection. The store is imperfect, financially precarious, and occasionally ridiculous, but it belongs to the people who inhabit it.The looming corporate takeover threatens more than a business. It threatens the characters’ sense of home.That’s what gives the story its emotional foundation. Saving Empire Records becomes a way of protecting the world they’ve built together.The Characters Feel Like People You Actually KnewOne of the movie’s greatest strengths is its ensemble cast. Rather than building the entire story around one protagonist, distributes its emotional weight across a collection of young people whose personalities, problems, and ambitions collide throughout the film.They’re exaggerated enough to be entertaining but recognizable enough to feel real.There’s Lucas, the impulsive employee whose attempt to save the store through a reckless gamble creates the crisis that drives the story. There’s Corey, the academically gifted overachiever whose carefully managed life begins to unravel under the pressure of expectations. Gina is confident, provocative, and determined to be taken seriously, even when she isn’t entirely sure what she wants.Debra is withdrawn and angry, carrying pain that her coworkers don’t fully understand. A.J. is an aspiring artist caught between romantic feelings and the uncertainty of pursuing a creative life. Warren, meanwhile, arrives as an outsider and quickly becomes part of the store’s increasingly chaotic orbit.Then there’s Mark, whose laid-back, slightly ridiculous personality provides some of the film’s funniest moments.What makes these characters work is that none of them has everything figured out. They possess different degrees of confidence, intelligence, sensitivity, and self-awareness, but they’re all struggling with something.Corey might look like the person most likely to succeed, but academic achievement doesn’t protect her from insecurity. Gina’s boldness doesn’t eliminate her need for validation. A.J.’s artistic ambitions don’t make difficult conversations any easier. Debra’s anger doesn’t tell the whole story of what she’s experiencing.These contradictions make the characters interesting.The movie doesn’t suggest that being young automatically makes someone profound or that every problem can be solved with a heartfelt speech. Instead, it presents a group of people who are frequently immature, selfish, confused, and occasionally wonderful.In other words, they’re believable.The genius is in allowing their personalities to clash without making every disagreement a moral lesson. They’re coworkers, friends, potential lovers, and occasional irritants. They don’t always understand one another, but their lives overlap enough that they gradually learn to care.For anyone who worked a job in their teens or early twenties, the dynamic feels remarkably familiar. There was always a Lucas, a Gina, a Corey, or a Mark somewhere in the building. There were friendships that made no sense on paper but worked perfectly in practice.And there was almost always someone who made an ordinary shift memorable.The Record Store Is the Real StarAlthough the characters carry the story, Empire Records itself is arguably the movie’s most important creation.The store represents a particular kind of cultural space that has become increasingly difficult to find. It’s a place where music is something you discover rather than something an algorithm delivers to you. You browse without necessarily knowing what you’re looking for. You pick up an album because the cover catches your eye. You ask an employee for a recommendation and end up discovering a band that changes your life.Music is personal in this environment. It isn’t simply background entertainment. It’s a way of expressing identity, finding community, and communicating feelings that are otherwise difficult to articulate.The employees understand this instinctively. Their musical interests help define who they are, and the store allows them to share those interests with one another.The movie also recognizes the social importance of independent businesses. Empire Records isn’t just competing on price or convenience. Its value comes from its personality, its employees, and the feeling that the place belongs to its community.A corporate chain might offer a more efficient business model, but efficiency isn’t the same thing as character.That conflict gives the film an unexpectedly enduring theme. The struggle between independent culture and corporate consolidation wasn’t invented in the 1990s, and it certainly hasn’t disappeared. It applies to record stores, bookstores, music venues, movie theaters, and countless other places where the personality of a business is inseparable from the people who make it special.The film doesn’t need to deliver a lecture about capitalism to make its point. It shows us what would be lost if Empire Records disappeared.We understand why these characters care because we’ve spent time inside their world.And that is much more effective than simply telling the audience that independent stores are important.The Soundtrack Is Practically Another CharacterAny discussion of that doesn’t give its soundtrack considerable attention is missing a major part of the movie’s identity.Music isn’t merely placed between scenes to keep the energy moving. It establishes the atmosphere, reveals character, and helps turn the store into a believable cultural universe.The soundtrack captures the alternative-rock sensibility of the mid-1990s, when grunge was still influencing popular culture, Britpop was finding a wider audience, and alternative music had become a dominant force among young listeners.The film’s musical selections create a recognizable sense of time without making the experience feel like a history lesson.Among the standout songs is the Gin Blossoms’ “Til I Hear It from You,” which became closely associated with the movie and reached a much wider audience through its connection to the film. The song captures the restless romantic energy of the story while fitting naturally into its broader musical identity.Then there’s the inclusion of “Sugarhigh” by Coyote Shivers, a perfect example of the movie’s willingness to embrace playful, slightly chaotic rock-and-roll energy.The soundtrack also benefits from the presence of artists such as The Cranberries, Better Than Ezra, and other performers associated with the alternative scene of the era. Together, they create an environment that feels lived in rather than artificially assembled.But the soundtrack’s real achievement is how naturally it connects music with personality.The characters don’t just happen to work in a record store. They’re people for whom music is part of the language they use to understand the world. Their tastes, attitudes, and emotional responses are shaped by the songs surrounding them.For audiences who grew up during the period, the music can trigger an almost physical sense of nostalgia. A song begins, and suddenly you’re remembering the clothes you wore, the people you knew, the places you went, and the albums you played until you practically wore them out.For younger viewers, the soundtrack offers a window into a time when discovering music often required a little more curiosity and a lot more wandering through record-store racks.The film’s musical identity is so strong that it would be difficult to imagine it working nearly as well without it.The songs don’t simply accompany the story.A Movie About Being Young Without Knowing What Comes NextBeneath the comedy, romance, and musical nostalgia, is fundamentally a story about uncertainty.The characters are standing at the edge of adulthood, but none of them has received a reliable instruction manual. They have ambitions, expectations, insecurities, and romantic fantasies, but the future remains frustratingly unclear.Corey is trying to meet expectations that may not even reflect what she truly wants. A.J. is wrestling with the vulnerability required to pursue his artistic ambitions and express his feelings. Gina is trying to reconcile the person she presents to the world with the person she wants to become.Debra’s struggles are more serious, giving the film an emotional dimension that extends beyond ordinary teenage confusion.These stories work because the movie understands that growing up isn’t a clean transition from ignorance to wisdom. It’s a process of making mistakes, recognizing your limitations, and occasionally discovering that the life you thought you wanted isn’t necessarily the life that will make you happy.The characters don’t suddenly become adults by the end of the movie. They’re still young, still impulsive, and still capable of making terrible decisions.What changes is their understanding of themselves and one another.They begin to recognize that the people around them are dealing with problems that aren’t always visible. Someone who appears confident may be desperately insecure. Someone who seems detached may be hurting. Someone who appears to have a perfect future may be terrified of it.That recognition creates empathy.And empathy, rather than maturity in the conventional sense, becomes one of the movie’s most important ideas.The film suggests that growing up involves learning to see other people more clearly, even when you haven’t quite figured yourself out.The Genius of Its Imperfect ToneOne reason has remained such a divisive movie is that its tone can be all over the place.It moves between broad comedy, romantic awkwardness, workplace chaos, emotional drama, and moments of genuine sadness. Some scenes are deliberately ridiculous. Others are surprisingly sincere. Occasionally, the movie shifts from one emotional register to another so quickly that it feels as though several different films are competing for the same running time.Its characters can be cartoonish. Some of its conflicts are resolved with a convenience that real life rarely provides. Certain moments lean heavily into the heightened emotional style of 1990s youth cinema.These are legitimate weaknesses.Yet the same qualities contribute to the film’s personality. feels messy because its characters are messy. Its emotional shifts reflect the intensity with which young people can experience life, when a disastrous afternoon feels like the end of the world and a great night with friends feels like the beginning of everything.The movie doesn’t always know when to be subtle, but it understands the emotional scale of being young.At that age, you can experience embarrassment, heartbreak, excitement, anger, and joy within the space of a single day. A minor humiliation can feel catastrophic. A romantic gesture can seem monumental. A friendship can become the most important thing in your life.The film captures that intensity through its restless pacing and occasionally excessive sentimentality.Its rough edges also prevent it from feeling too polished or corporate. There’s an appealing scruffiness to the whole enterprise, an impression that the movie is more interested in its characters than in maintaining perfect narrative discipline.Not every scene lands. Not every joke works. Not every character receives the development they deserve.But the movie has a pulse.And sometimes, personality is more valuable than perfection.Why the Movie Became a Cult ClassicThe history of is part of what makes its legacy so interesting.The movie was not initially received as the generational touchstone it would eventually become. Its theatrical performance was disappointing, and its reputation grew through later viewings, home video, cable television, and the gradual accumulation of devoted fans.That evolution reflects something important about the way audiences connect with movies.A film can fail to make an immediate impression and still find the right people at the right time. Sometimes a movie’s most important audience isn’t the one that sees it on opening weekend. It’s the audience that discovers it years later, when the characters’ experiences suddenly feel personal.For many viewers, became a movie associated with a particular period of life. They watched it with friends, quoted its dialogue, memorized its soundtrack, and returned to it whenever they wanted to revisit the atmosphere of the 1990s.The film also benefited from the strength of its central setting. A record store is a remarkably effective place to build a coming-of-age story because it brings together people with different personalities while giving them a shared interest.The characters have somewhere to go, something to do, and a reason to spend time together. Their lives intersect naturally, without requiring the plot to manufacture an elaborate excuse for every encounter.That makes the movie easy to revisit. Even when viewers know exactly how the story unfolds, they can return simply to spend time with the characters.This is one of the defining qualities of a cult classic: the pleasure isn’t limited to discovering what happens next. It’s about returning to a world you enjoy inhabiting.The movie’s cultural afterlife has also been sustained by the music, the fashion, the dialogue, and its association with an era that now feels both familiar and distant.For those who experienced the 1990s firsthand, it offers a concentrated dose of nostalgia. For viewers who came later, it provides an appealing portrait of a pre-streaming music culture built around physical spaces, shared discoveries, and personal recommendations.Its imperfections haven’t prevented it from becoming beloved.In some ways, they’ve helped.The Movie Understands the Importance of Finding Your PeoplePerhaps the most emotionally resonant element of is its belief that people don’t have to be perfect to matter to one another.The employees are an unlikely collection of personalities. They don’t always agree, and they certainly don’t always behave well. They make impulsive decisions, hurt one another’s feelings, and occasionally create problems that would be easier to solve if everyone simply acted like a reasonable adult.But they keep showing up.They share a workplace, a passion for music, and an increasingly urgent reason to work together. Over time, those connections become more meaningful than their differences.The film’s emotional payoff depends on the audience believing that this group of people genuinely cares about one another.
