item.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. (: also online multiplayer; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!)Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse hereDifferent weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possibleArea effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer with bonus resourcesIn-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks outDifferent in-game (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) mode, to watch those personalities play each otherThe - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base that add extra rules or twistsRanks and achievements () mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each otherA based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp PongBattle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.v1: the initial prototypeI started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resourcesLet's start with a MVP design, ask me some questionsHere's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play.Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later!The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this:This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play.I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as:A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.This kicked off of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.v5: Battle Drones goes 3DAfter the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious:Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapesThe new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft.I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases.I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them.It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.This resulted in my longest prompt yet:Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different placesI want to encourage a battle over uplinks.The map should be the times the size of other maps - still squareFirst research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modificationsYou get to design a new biome for thisThe result was the tropical map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this:v10: Goliath, and agent battlesI decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yetLet's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be.Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troopsDamage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it[...] Lets do two condors can carry the mechThe end result is .Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map.Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area.Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map!The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building any Goliaths they might have built.There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths: starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units. adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one).The other v10 feature is . In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game?Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...]Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools pluginThere are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future.This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target:Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.Here's the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work:v12: Multiplayer via soundI only got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other!This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept:Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signalsBuild a version of that for battledronesOpus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well!Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game.I know almost about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results.Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!A few other observations from this project:Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached.Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to and and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked.Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of fame).Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.I'm still not quite over the of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.Update: Online multiplayer supportEarlier in this article I said:Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache!That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead:If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance?Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folderHere's the resulting server. Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time.Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code.I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game.I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative.

item.title: The Pelicans Broke How I Understand Pro Basketball
item.author: Corban Goble
item.content:encoded: It's unlikely that you spend much time thinking about the New Orleans Pelicans. However, as a New Orleans resident for whom ball is life, I am rather fixated on them. This team is far stranger than you may have previously understood. They suck in a singular way, and I’ve convinced myself to love them for it. No one else is doing it quite like this.Any attention that was paid to the Pelicans by the broader NBA community last season was a result of one of the strangest trades in NBA history. This, you probably are familiar with: During the 2025 NBA draft, freshly installed Pelicans executives Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver traded an unprotected 2026 first-round pick in order to move up 10 slots and take Derik Queen at No. 13. The Pels have picked Queen at No. 7, which would have aligned with the organization’s internal valuation of him, but instead they decided to give up an extremely valuable future pick for a smiley, versatile big man who absolutely cannot play defense. The pick they gave up became a top-three selection for the Indiana Pacers in a consensus three-player draft in 2026, but thanks to some ping-pong balls, it instead became the eighth pick and remained with the Atlanta Hawks. So who’s laughing now? The Weaver-Dumars partnership is a particularly thrilling thread of this team’s current construction. Dumars—who last held an operations job for an NBA franchise in 2020, when he performed several jobs for the Sacramento Kings—worked at the NBA’s league office in Secaucus until the Pelicans hired him in 2025. In Detroit, where he last held a GM role, he flamed out spectacularly. Weaver also previously held the GM job in Detroit, and while he and Dumars never worked together, they arrived together in New Orleans as a kind of package deal. As GM of the Pistons from 2020-24, Weaver built rosters that compiled a 74-244 record. On his podcast, John Hollinger has called Weaver a “subcontractor” in the Pels' GM job, effectively just being the right arm of Dumars.

item.title: The Guardians Were And Are A Drag
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: The Cleveland Guardians will not win the World Series this autumn, just as they have not in any of the last 78 autumns. They were eliminated Monday night by the Tampa Bay Rays: outslugged, out-small-balled, and outlasted. Thus ends what was, by regular-season record, an uneven and dreary but still somehow typical year for the Guardians, who have won between 46 percent and 63 percent of their games every season for 14 years running. In terms of proximity to a championship, this was the most successful Guardians season since 2016, when they made the World Series and fell in seven games to the Chicago Cubs."We won another division," said a gloomy Austin Hedges after his Guardians were eliminated Monday night. "That's really cool. We won a playoff series. That's really cool." Hedges was hurting, and his point was that the objective coolness of these accomplishments would eventually penetrate his disappointment and give him a sense of satisfaction.Unfortunately for Hedges, almost nothing about the Guardians can be honestly described as "cool." In the realm of aesthetics and vibes, let me say this much: I am glad I do not have to watch any more Guardians games between now and next summer. It's not that I bear them any specific ill will: Unlike at least one of my Defector colleagues, I am not pursuing an active personal vendetta against Steven Kwan. But as the Rays ascended in this ALCS—and as a consequence of the particular way that they ascended, by being better than the Guardians both where the Guardians are weak (hitting the ball hard, hitting the ball in the air) and where the Guardians are strong (posting crooked numbers without ever making solid contact)—they began to exude what I think of as the good kind of inevitability. Tampa Bay's guys were cool and cocky, they seemed downright saturated with juice, and at regular intervals they did bitchin' things. They seemed dialed to the moment, which is to say like a team that belonged in the World Series.

item.title: The Best Monopoly Strategy, Tested on 300 Million Games
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I turned eight classic Monopoly strategies into computer players and made them play 312,898,560 games against each other. At a table of four, the best one won 43% of its games. The worst one won 3%.The gap doesn’t come from one clever trick. It comes from four common mistakes: being picky about what you buy, saving your cash, stopping at three houses, and refusing to trade. Then I let the computer tune every habit at once, to see how far a carefully tuned player can go and which color set is really worth fighting for.P.S. I don’t actually play Monopoly anymore — it is the world’s most maddening game (along with Sorry) and I childishly refer to it as “Monotony” — and an aside about 3 minutes into the video is why: “roughly one game in six never ends”. Exactly! And you want me to haggle? For fun? No thank you. I imagine there are folks whose idea of a good time is visiting used car dealerships for funsies when they don’t need a car, but I am not one of them.

item.title: Mana Shim Walked Away From Soccer, Then She Rebuilt Her Life
item.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
item.content:encoded: Five years ago this fall, The Athletic published a feature in which NWSL players Mana Shim and Sinead Farrelly opened up about their abusive former Portland Thorns coach, Paul Riley. The story prompted an investigation into how the NWSL handled reports of abuse, and by the end of that year, half of the league's head coaches either resigned or were fired, along with league commissioner Lisa Baird.I met Shim while on tour for in 2023, and I was curious to talk to her about how she made the decision to go public with her experiences when there are so many reasons not to, like the fragility of the then-nascent league and the potential repercussions she might experience. And there were the identity questions. She had dedicated her entire life to soccer, so what happened when she decided to walk away? How did she find her way back on new terms after everything that had happened?This season finale of is a bit heavier than the other episodes this season, but I wanted to end on it because I was so inspired by Shim's courage, not only to make herself vulnerable by speaking up, but in daring to imagine a new version of her life after spending so many years chasing a singular goal.

item.title: Death & Domains
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: A recent piece on “forever domains” sparked bigger questions about permanence online: when domain owners die out, do we need new systems that don't rely on domains at all?Should domains last forever? That’s not a new question for me, but it’s one that I’ve been thinking more about lately, especially since I ended up writing a story recently that posed this exact question.Over at the new publication GraveSite, which covers the concept of death and grief with a reporter’s eye, I posed a question I’ve thought a lot about over the years: How can you keep a person’s digital identity alive even if their physical identity is long gone? For corporate entities this is actually reasonably easy—succession plans and all that, ensuring someone is paying the bills long-term.But people aren‘t corporations, and business structures like domain registrars and web hosts often treat us as consumers. Which means that when we aren’t around to consume, and to pay money in exchange for that consumption, we’re going to be the first to lose our digital plot in the ground. There’s no internet cemetery, and we have a relatively limited number of archives that can hold our digital histories.Which means that, when we go offline, so will our digital identities, eventually. It’ll take longer, but that credit card isn’t going to pay for itself. If you’re a writer or creative, this is a real risk, and the answers for solving this simply aren’t very good.My piece goes over some of the novel solutions out there, including a nonprofit initiative to essentially take ownership of websites and pay the bills in your absence.I’m happy with the piece, but don’t want to spoil it, so I’ll simply encourage you to read. But I wanted to spend a second thinking about a the second-order effects of this: If domains last forever, at what point do we need to start over?This was an argument I heard from a couple of readers about this topic. There’s a finite number of domains—at what point are the domains already here going to crowd out people that left a long time ago. I own the domain erniesmith.net that I use to promote my freelance work; if I decided to sell it to a service that aims to keep a domain around “forever,” am I screwing over later generations of Ernie Smiths?It’s hard to say, but I do think it speaks to a longer-term architecture problem that the internet will eventually face, a crossroads as our domain owners die out, the domain maybe not being relevant anymore but their websites certainly having some value. And maybe the solution to this problem is to create new systems for distributing information online that don’t necessarily rely on domains.One commenter on my post, Alex Russell (a former Google Chrome engineer now working on Microsoft Edge), pointed to the idea of Web Packages, a concept where websites could be distributed in full without the need for any attached domain or even expected online access.It was an idea that originated with the Chrome team, but found little to no uptake with other browser-makers, eventually falling into the abyss of Web standards obscurities. (The project currently lives with the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG).) It arguably deserves to be revisited as the problem of dead websites and dead owners becomes a bigger problem. For one thing, it helps to resolve some of the bigger, more annoying problems with old websites—that they’re often required to be static when they’ve fallen into disuse, that they often don’t support https like modern sites do, and that they can carry latent security issues, much like how an old book can grow dust and mold if not managed properly. (In fact, one of the listed uses for web packages is to create an easy-to-distribute format for researching security exploits.)Should the domain system itself be seen as temporary? Should we treat old websites more like books whose volumes can be picked up at will when all is said and done? That’s a provocative idea, and one that I think deserves more discussion in the current climate.But one thing I’ll say is that our system is completely upside down if your website stands a better chance of being around in 100 years if it’s a Facebook profile or a forgotten Blogger or LiveJournal site than if you put in the work to carefully put it on the internet yourself.Anyway, I look forward to talking about these issues with the GraveSite team on October 27, when If this topic at all appeals to you, hope to see you there. Get ready for some drama, folks. has a feature explaining what, exactly, happened with Matt Mullenweg last month when he very briefly was booted from his CEO role with Automattic. As you might guess, it has to do with the ongoing WP Engine mess. to friend of Tedium Sean Malseed, a.k.a. Action Retro, who publicly discussed his health issues with his audience. That stuff isn’t fun, and he’s not all the way through it, but I’m glad he’s still with us. After all, someone needs to put Haiku on a toaster, and I’d prefer if he did it.Tying to my prior discussion of ArtCraft, I think that the rising trend of reverse engineering of technology you already own is a good thing, especially when it counters ugly corporate practices. Smart TVs, as highlighted by , are an excellent starting point here.

item.title: Angel Reese Crafted Her Masterpiece
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Like its sludgy predecessor and by design, Game 2 of the WNBA Finals was played as if in the mud. Clean dribbling of the ball was prohibited, the two participants collaborated on 33 turnovers, and the Atlanta Dream finished one missed three-pointer beyond joining the Golden State Valkyries with an identical, gross 21-for-61 shooting night. Ballhalla's famous resolve was tested, as its stars spent the night dribbling sideways for 23 seconds before hoisting terrible shots. But through it all, directly in the middle of the fray on both ends of the court, there was one player who gradually revealed herself to be the game's protagonist, the one gleefully forcing the Valks down into the mud. There was Angel Reese, dominating the biggest game of her career and seizing control of the WNBA Finals for her team.The stats tell some of the story: Reese finished with 30 points, 16 rebounds, and two blocks, got to the line 11 times, and finished as the only Atlanta player who made at least half their shot attempts. But the way her dominance was felt in the building was truly remarkable. Reese may as well have been the only player on the court. The San Francisco crowd puts a little extra energy into booing Reese, not out of a sense of culture-war conscription the way, say, an Indiana crowd would, but rather because she causes them the most pain.Both these Finals teams are set up with the primary objective of preventing opponents from playing basketball, which played out for everyone in Game 1 and for the Valkyries in Game 2. Reese was the one player who was getting anything easy: If she got a touch with momentum or against anyone who wasn't Kiah Stokes, she was getting to the rim. If she pulled down an offensive rebound, the Valks may as well have started setting up their offense at the other end. In a series otherwise entirely populated with people moving sideways, Reese is direct. When she's on the court, she demands attention.

item.title: It’s the AI Economy … We’re Just Living In It
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I corresponded with a TPM Reader from the tech world recently who marveled at the political salience of data centers when data centers have been around since the late 90s. Many data centers today are orders of magnitude larger than their pre-AI relatives, gobbling up much more energy, making more noise and physical pollution. But he noted that the bulk of them aren’t nearly that large. These points each have some truth to them, though I think it understates the real-world impact of hyperscaler data centers. And, as I’ve noted, a lot of our collective social angst about data centers and AI is really focused on oligarchy — the way that it appears to be the tech oligarchs’ world and we’re just living in it. The ability for town and county councils to say no to data centers is irresistible precisely because it’s the one case where democratic self-government is in a position to say “NO!” and that’s so contrary to all our other experience these days. But there’s an entirely different vantage point on this question I want to focus on.The impact of particular data centers in particular places is one issue. But the macro-story is even bigger and more jarring. Axios has a piece this morning about how the housing sector is getting hammered by the hyperscaler AI boom, both buildings and buyers. And as you may have heard the lack of affordable housing is a rather pressing issue in American society today. This applies to everything from inflation/scarcity of the physical building blocks that are used for building housing to the scarcity of capital to fund it. If that sounds overstated look at this chart from a study we discussed late last month and which got written up in various publications.

item.title: Polymarket Was Allowing Bets On Sexual Assault Cases Until People Started Asking Questions
item.author: Diana Moskovitz
item.content:encoded: For nearly three weeks, a real bet a person could place on the Polymarket gambling app was on "Any of the Cornell 7 charged with a felony sex crime?" The Cornell 7 refers to seven defendants in a civil lawsuit filed last month by a former Cornell University student who said she was gang-raped by several fraternity members.No criminal charges have been filed, but after the lawsuit drew national attention, a local prosecutor said on Sept. 28 that his office would reopen the criminal investigation. Two days later, on Sept. 30, a market opened up on the popular gambling platform (though technically it is a "prediction market") to bet on the results of the investigation. The market was not available to bettors in the United States version of the app, but the bet itself was very easy to find. I just punched "Cornell 7" into the search bar and found it pretty easily.

item.title: Some Wins Feel More Like Losses
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Without knowing for sure whether this is actually true, we can still surmise that the Washington Commanders felt better about losing Monday night's game than they did about their delightfully grotesque tie against the Giants in Week 5. And we are almost certain the San Francisco 49ers felt worse in victory. Their record stayed spotless, but in making their escape, they caught a glimpse of the grim future that is in their front yard.If you chose to avoid last night's Commanders–49ers game in the shadows of Hell's Substation, you are finding out today what happens when the scoreboard lies, and also when it becomes permissible to lie about the scoreboard. The practical truth is that the 49ers won 23-17, and remain one of the NFL's three undefeated teams. The victory broadened their lead in the NFC West to half the schedule—a margin of three games over the barely tenable Seattle Seahawks after six weeks of action. The math here is nearly unassailable, but hold on a moment while we assail it.By losing, the Commanders managed not only to drop from 1-4-1, the fourth-worst record in the sport, but to complete a second consecutive week of winless football from the entire NFC East. Those divisional rivals pulled together to lose six games outright and tie a seventh in humiliating fashion. This is the first time an entire division has gone without a single team winning in back-to-back weeks since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, and almost certainly the first time ever, though we suspect nobody is bored enough to give that research a go. Only one team in the division, the New York Giants, has a winning record, and none of them have a positive point differential. After six weeks, the NFC East has fashioned itself as a hideous homage to the American League West, the new standard for no standards at all.

item.title: The Trump DOJ Is Now the Greatest Threat to Free and Fair Elections
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Open and Ongoing RatfuckeryThe Trump DOJ — corruptly deployed by the White House as an unprecedented election interference tool — sure is getting the headlines it wants from its campaign to prosecute alleged noncitizen voting while the midterm elections are already underway:NYT: Justice Dept. Charges 28 in California With Voting-Related CrimesAP: Justice Department arrests more than 2 dozen in California sweep targeting alleged noncitizen votersNPR: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalateEven though those stories include the usual caveats — about the rarity of noncitizen voting, Trump’s track record of inflating the risks thereof, and the administration’s disinformation campaign targeting the election — the top-line news remains arrests and prosecutions.DOJ says it has charged 113 people in 20 states with illegal voting and illegal registration offenses over the last seven weeks.The timing is no accident, of course.Rolling out alleged noncitizen voting prosecutions right before the election instills fear in Black and brown communities, may dampen voter turnout, provides a ready-made excuse for GOP losses, serves as a pretext for challenging/delegitimizing the election results, and generally is a brazen display of ratfuckery.The DOJ has not been discreet or muted in its approach. It has issued press releases touting its noncitizen voting prosecutions that contain photos of the defendants (albeit with their faces digitally obscured). Yesterday, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter held a press conference in California — where mail-in voting is already underway — to announce the 28 new prosecutions there, which DOJ has dubbed “Operation Protect the Vote.”The arrests weren’t low-key either. The wife of a 72-year-old man from Belize said federal agents showed up at their house before dawn in full tactical gear with guns drawn — along with camera crews and news helicopters. He later appeared in court still in his pajamas. He is reportedly a registered Republican.The timing is especially glaring because some of the new alleged noncitizen voting cases go back years, to 2020 and earlier. A couple of the new California cases allege fraudulent voter registration as far back as 2002 and 2003. Some of the cases don’t even allege illegal voting per se, but rather making false statements on naturalization paperwork. One lawful permanent resident charged in North Carolina has been in the United States for so long that DOJ identifies her as a “national of former Yugoslavia.”Why The Timing Is Extra PerniciousBut the timing isn’t accidental for another reason: Bringing these cases so late in the cycle leaves no time to test these allegations in court before the election. If the cases later fall apart, if they’re dismissed, if they result in acquittals, then … too bad, so sad.The attempted prosecutions will have served their election disinformation purposes, and there’s no way to roll back the clock and undo the damage.There are already early signs that some of the new prosecutions in California are flimsy. Some of the newly charged immigrants said they had no memory of ever registering to vote, the LA Times reported:At the federal courthouse in downtown Los Angeles late Monday, several green card holders arrested in a crackdown on alleged California voter fraud expressed confusion over the charges — with some saying they had no recollection of registering to vote, as Trump administration officials accuse them of doing.Among them was Ana Domínguez, 60, a native of El Salvador living in Long Beach as a lawful permanent resident. Federal authorities accused her Monday of fraudulently registering to vote in July 2006 and then lying about it in her naturalization paperwork in March 2026.Domínguez said she did not have any memory of registering to vote.Another man accused of the same crimes as Domínguez said the same: He wasn’t aware of ever registering to vote, as federal prosecutors claimed he had.It’s not uncommon for noncitizens to end up being unknowingly registered to vote during previous interactions with the government. “There is only a crime if the government can prove willful violations of federal law,” election law expert Rich Hasen noted.DOJ’s One-Two California PunchThe new round of criminal cases is happening in parallel with the Trump DOJ’s lawsuit against California trying to force it to segregate and not count alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots — again, while voting is already happening.The administration continues to try to ratchet up pressure on California election officials. In a letter Friday, the DOJ reportedly warned that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation.In a striking admission, acting DAG McCotter, the DOJ’s No. 2, conceded yesterday that the list of some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters that the administration is demanding California use to segregate ballots may contain some citizens:Ultimately, the most pernicious aspect of this campaign against the phantom scourge of noncitizen voting is the risk that the administration’s sloppiness, indifference, and aggressiveness results in legally cast ballots from U.S. citizens not being counted.In a 180-degree turn, the Justice Department has gone from its historic role of protecting and defending the individual right to vote to being the leading threat to free and fair elections.I remain puzzled why so much of the Trump administration’s election-interference and disinformation campaign is focused on California. The electoral math doesn’t add up. Thoughts?A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.This scheme appears to have never gotten off the ground.WaPo: A small group of about 10 current and former U.S. national security officials with DoD experience has been discreetly advising state governments and members of Congress on how to prepare for the possibility that the Trump administration will attempt to interfere in November’s midterm elections.“Our number one risk at this point is the federal government.”—Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold (D) on the biggest threat to free and fair electionsPure Unadulterated Racism

item.title: ‘Barbara Forever’ Won’t Let You Forget
item.author: Sohini Desai
item.content:encoded: After listening to a critique of the Miss America pageant on a public radio station, Barbara Hammer declared herself a feminist. Then she left her husband. Then she became a lesbian. This was the early 1970s, and it wasn’t long before someone gifted baby gay Hammer a Super-8 and she commenced pointing it—lovingly, relentlessly—at every human crease and crevice in her life. Around this time, Hammer started writing down her name and address and placing them in balloons for others to find. “Otherwise I’d be lost in the world,” she said of the practice in an “exit interview,” given just before she died in 2019. Brydie O’Connor’s is one of these balloons: a documentary worthy of its iconic subject, that captures and arranges fragments of Barbara for us to turn over in our hands. It’s a devoted, sincere ode to the avant-garde artist, who, as she put it, made movies out of sex and life—more than 80 of them, to be a little more precise, over the course of half a century. Hammer filmed herself and her personal relationships obsessively, creating the vast archive that serves as the basis of . At the beginning of the film, there’s a series of images of Hammer pointing a camera into a passing window, or the rearview mirror of a car or motorcycle, her left eye squinting, her right looking into a viewfinder. We often see Barbara holding and speaking directly to the camera in the documentary, creating the uncanny sense that she made it herself, from beyond the grave. Though Hammer narrates the entire documentary, the narrative is pieced together from various sources. Barbara’s voice will sound effortful and aged at one moment, then youthful and mischievous in the next. O’Connor also replicates her subject’s love of a match cut, folding together images from throughout Hammer’s career. The result is not the chronology of a life, but the story of a filmmaker—starting when Barbara first picked up a camera, and ending with who she became to others. It’s a story of self-creation and self-plunder, of Barbara inventing herself and using her life as the raw material of her artistry.

item.title: Same rally, different day: Welcome to the worst version of Groundhog Day ever, starring Preznit Fuckwit
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Same shit, different day.It’s a well-worn phrase, but it’s never been truer than this election cycle. Every goddamed day is like waking up into a farce that quickly devolves into the most fucked-up version of Groundhog Day ever. Lucky us — we get to watch the entire Donnyerse pull the same stupid shit, over and over and over and over. Monday was no different. It checked every single box. Buckle in, and let us document the atrocities.Did the day begin with some nonsensical Oval Bordello dog-and-pony show? Shouldn’t Donny have figured out by now that any attempt at affection is going to result with him being on the wrong end of a public humiliation?Melania was there to introduce who the fuck even knows what she there to introduce. We keep hearing about how this woman speaks five languages, but English is apparently not one of them. “…also establishes the The White House Women’s— Health Task Force, which will— mobilize the entire federal government to coordinate action focused on improving women’s health. And this task force will be led by Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy, that’s a big one. And, uh, he’s been fantastic.”Fact check: has Bobby Brainworms indeed been ‘fantastic’?I have no idea what this so-called ‘women’s health task force’ is supposed to achieve, but I do know that every time Cokesnort McToiletseat rears his head, some long-ago-conquered, easily-preventable malady makes a roaring comeback.You’re welcome, women! Enjoy the who-knows-what-delights that are in store for you. Probably dying during childbirth.After the dog-and-pony show, did Donny commit a dumbfuck, all over his piece-of-shit app? New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America! The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag! Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!President DONALD J. TRUMPCan you fucking believe that this infantile garbage was posted by a grown-ass adult? Does our Slumlord-in-Chief actually believe that property values in Albuquerque are suppressed because the word ‘Mexico’ is in the state’s name? Apparently he does. Every day, this idiot out-stupids himself over some obsession that no one else on the planet gives one corroded shit about, and we’re all expected to pretend it never happened. What the fuck? I know I’ve been over-using this gif lately, but it so perfectly encapsulates our current national moment.We all know exactly how Kate Walsh feels: After shitting his nonsense all over Social Media, did Dear Leader once again betray one of our allies, while waddling to his beloved Epstein Helipad? Trump: “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much.”Fact check: has Russia been ?Today, Russian drones and missiles hit the capital without warning, leaving walls slashed by shrapnel, blowing out residences, a shopping mall, and a school, part of Russia's attempt to make Kyiv unlivable.No matter what atrocities Russia commits, Donny’s assignment is to insist that it’s all a no-biggie. Did Donny then jet off to another hate-rally in , they’re all exactly the same? Trump: “The first one is they show you a lion, a bear, a snake, and a giraffe. And they say, ‘Which one is the giraffe?’ I got a perfect score.”Trump on Iran: “We’re knocking the shit out of them ... we could leave right now”I don’t know about you, but I’m fucking exhausted by all the winning.Trump: “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I'm not going it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him. That’s a big deal for Kansas.”Trump on Christianity: “I know more than anybody…A certain pastor said…’He's going to lead us to a period of time in Christianity that nobody else can do — that nobody else can do.’ And he turned out to be right.”Big, strong Christians with tears in their eyes, going ‘Sir! Sir! How do you do it? No one religions like you do! Sir!”Trump refers to President Xi as “China.”Okay, but did Donny do a racism? Check, check, and check — because Donny did a shitload of racisms.“Trump says the press smeared Roger Marshall as ‘a Shylock type guy’”Shylock! Now there’s an antisemitic deep cut.Shylock, of course, is the Jewish moneylender invented by William Shakespeare in 1596 — which we all know was an awesome time to be a Jew in Europe. By the early 20th century in America, to call someone a ‘Shylock’ was to imply that they were as greedy and dishonest as one of them-there types. No doubt, it’s a slur that Donny learned from his tyrant Klansman father. Thing is, nobody’s hurled that term as in insult in probably forty or fifty years. It’s gone out of fashion — but Donny’s too decrepit to remember that we don’t say that any more, in polite company.I’m still waiting for Donny to blurt the n-word into an open microphone. You know it’s only a matter of time.While Dear Leader was waddling across his beloved Epstein Helipad toward Helicopter Force One, he stopped to acknowledge and wave at— well, we have no idea what was going on inside Donny’s collapsed cortex. At the 21-second mark, as the camera pulls back, we learn that he was waving at .Now, I want you to cast your mind back to June of 2024, when Joe Biden was in Italy for a G7 meeting.Joe — who, you’ll remember, was alleged to be old and icky and smelled bad and was probably already dead but too demented to realize it — appeared to wander off aimlessly, right smack in the middle of an event. The right-wing noise machine had a fucking field day with it.Fast forward two and a half years. We have actual, recorded, evidence of Dear Leader waving at an imaginary crowd that exists only inside his rat-infested head, and not worthless scribbler of the corporate-controlled press can be roused from their slumbers to mention it.Why the hell not? Isn’t that newsworthy?Now let’s do the best part of our National Groundhog Day — the Daily Claudia.Here’s a triptych of Katie and her mom in Fort Davis, Texas, on April 20, 2022.Have a great Tuesday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Documentation-Driven Development
item.content:encoded: Last week, I needed to make some pretty major updates to a web component in a design system I use for clients.I decided the easiest thing to do was document how the new component would work… before actually writing any code to implement the updates.It was an entirely ADHD-driven decision, but it unlocked something for me! Writing the docs forced me to think about the component would work: customizations I’d want to include, default settings, backwards compatibility, and so on.This made writing the tests far easier, which then made writing the code easier.I’m certainly the first person to come up with idea of Documentation-Driven Development, but I definitely want to try this approach again.

item.title: I Love The Colorful Stars
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: A Weird Star is a classic place-setter in fiction. Put a Weird Star in the sky, even if it never has anything to do with the plot, and you know we're somewhere different and alien. Anything that's clearly not our Sun, and you're cooking with gas. Maybe it's a binary system, and there's two suns. Maybe it's large and looming. Maybe it's even flickering, like Jack Vance used, to excellent effect. But rarely do authors fuck around with color. A star is white, or red if it's going out soon, or, if the planet is question is truly fucked, the star is blue because that's the hottest color there is. Those are the colors of stars, we figured. Not even sci-fi authors could conceive of a mechanism to get some new tints in there.As is often the case, the real universe turns out to be stranger than imagination. Stars, under the right circumstances, can appear to observers on their orbiting planets in a wide spectrum of colors, from hot pink to the green of cucumber lime Gatorade. "Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star," said Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick and lead author on the study. I'm imagining it, Mark! It rocks!The paper, published last week in RAS Techniques and Instruments, doesn't rely on having found some new stars lit up like Christmas lights. Instead, it's a breakthrough in modeling. Traditionally, stars are modeled as putting out black-body radiation. Black bodies are mathematical conveniences, idealized objects: perfectly opaque and non-reflective, and emitting light in all wavelengths. Black bodies do not actually exist, but stars are close enough to that the models work for most purposes, which is the important thing. In black-body radiation, light will only ever vary depending on the temperature of the object, going from red to white to blue as the object gets hotter. Play around with the burners on your stove to grasp this immediately.

item.title: How Japanese Dried Bonito Is Made
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: How katsuobushi — Japanese dried bonito, said to be the world’s hardest food — is made in Nishi-Izu, Japan. Inside Kanesa Katsuobushi Shoten, a workshop founded in 1882, 5th-generation craftsman Yasuhisa Serizawa still uses the 200-year-old “tebiyama” hand-fired smoke-drying method that only a few workshops in Japan preserve. Watch fresh bonito being filleted and boiled for 90 minutes, smoke-dried more than 10 times over a hand-tended wood fire, repaired with bonito paste, fermented with koji mold and sun-dried for months — over half a year until the fish becomes as hard as wood and shines like a jewel. From fresh catch to katsuobushi.This method of making dried bonito flakes has been used in the Tago district of West Izu for a long time, and its history is said to date back about 300 years (to the Edo period). It involves digging a vertical hole about 2 meters deep, burning firewood (raw wood from Izu: oak, sawtooth oak, cherry, etc.) from the bottom of the hole, and smoking and drying the dried bonito flakes with the high temperature of an open flame. This method is called the Tebiyama-shiki smoking method. It is the oldest existing smoking method, and only a few bonito flake manufacturers in the country continue to use this method to make dried bonito flakes, so it is said to be a legendary method. The Tebiyama-shiki smoking method is said to produce dried bonito flakes with a rich flavor because the surface of the bonito is smoked all at once with the high temperature of an open flame, locking in the umami.

item.title: Rayfabe
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: Here’s an incomplete list of things that happened after Junior Caminero, the 23-year-old Rays slugger, hit what appeared to be a back-breaking two-run homer off the foul pole in the seventh inning of ALCS Game 6:Short of and to the crowd side of first base, Caminero stopped, leaned back, closed his eyes and pounded his chest with both fists — a move reminiscent of Disney movie Tarzan.He cupped his hand to his ear rounding second, imploring the Tropicana Field crowd to keep roaring.In the top of the eighth, Guardians star Jose Ramirez popped out weakly to center field, and then sat defeated on the dugout bench, straining to envision a different outcome on the ceiling, in the depths of his head.But then … Chase DeLauter beat out a grounder to first. Nathaniel Lowe singled. The Rays brought in Ian Seymour to pitch. He promptly walked Travis Bazzana and and Patrick Bailey, then plunked Angel Martinez, forcing in two runs. The Caminero homer was essentially erased.Another pitching change got the Rays out of the jam, still up two.Shortly thereafter, Diaz, baseball’s reigning god of protein, consumed a tomahawk steak like an ice cream cone during the clubhouse celebration.The Rays are going to the World Series, and they made a meal out of it.What little I know about professional wrestling, I have absorbed accidentally. But the final two frames of the ALCS were unmistakable. A haymaking blow from a main character, full minutes of time spent celebrating and heralding that split-second achievement, a rapid series of barely believable events rendering that triumph essentially moot, a new haymaker thrown, a coronation, a promo cut on the microphone.Maybe it’s the sheer size of Caminero and Diaz. Maybe it’s the color pop of the Devil Rays alternate uniforms Tampa has adopted for this run. Maybe it’s the freezer-aisle-at-Costco lighting of Tropicana Field. This baseball game became pro wrestling. And that felt good, actually, felt right.Tampa Bay has fielded successful teams many, many times without necessarily filling the rafters at the poorly placed dome in St. Petersburg, and often without inspiring more admiration than what you’d offer for a particularly onerous mathematical advancement. The Rays’ deep postseason runs, though, have come with extra park-adjusted oomph that animates their excellence — a sort of lie that amplifies the truth. What I’ve come to understand as .In wrestling, kayfabe is the art of fully buying into the fiction for an audience that knows the production is staged. The baseball isn’t staged, but there’s value in extracting the unspoken tension trapped in scorecards and clenched jaw muscles and firing it out of a T-shirt cannon into plain sight, onto the field.It’s charisma and catharsis layered on top of the careful execution.Like Arozarena before him, Caminero is bringing the Rayfabe. Play-by-play announcer Brian Anderson said this during the post-homer rancor, but you might have missed it: That was the first homer anyone has ever hit off Cade Smith’s splitter in major-league action, regular or postseason, the lone long ball out of 884 pitches.Cartoon adaptations are possible throughout the clubhouse — Chandler Simpson’s speed; Victor Mesa Jr.’s rocket arm and little-brother-made-good story; the pitching staff of untouchable everyman clones; Diaz’s stoic, cuddly bodybuilder persona — that build on the productive, precise skills underneath. With two 40-homer seasons under his belt at, again, the age of 23, Caminero is the face. He’s a craftsman and a hype man.Under new ownership and plotting a move, at long last, to a more conveniently located ballpark, a moment like this is bigger for the Rays than it would be for most other clubs. A decade or more of front office mastery wins a lot of games, but doesn’t necessarily inspire the legions. I’d like to think this sort of display, packed into just a few weeks, could move that latter needle.It was fascinating that Arozarena, an impending free agent who has been with the Seattle Mariners, and Tyler Glasnow, a Rays avatar turned Dodgers starter, were in the stands to support the franchise. Glasnow, who departed after 2023, was teammates with Caminero for all of seven games. Arozarena was there a half-season longer, but still had only marginal time with what’s now the core of this group.Despite the constant churn, the packed bags and the often half-full dome, there’s a longer-term tale in Tampa. They help players find the best versions of themselves, help them identify and unleash something inside. Something about that connection clearly sticks for the guys who have been there and left. You wonder if someday, with more money or more support or more of whatever it will take to achieve either of those things, it might manifest itself in ways that go beyond just Rays.I don’t know what ending I’d script for the franchise’s Tropicana Field era.In the dome, you can sense that the conditions are weird and subpar, but also special. Every iota of attention is earned and paid off. The show has to be fully mustered from the talents of the performers. There’s an underdog quality, even when they are clearly the best team in the American League.Another thing I’ve picked up about wrestling: The crowd’s favorite doesn’t always win, but a strong character development can alter the future.The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: Rays Clinch Ultimate Thrifter World Series
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: For a moment there, it was getting a bit sleepy. In the bottom of the seventh inning, the Tampa Bay Rays were up 3-1 on the Cleveland Guardians: a lead, but not an insurmountable one. Each of their three runs came from plinking away at the Guardians' relievers—the Guardians were reduced to a bullpen game to fend off elimination—in the second and third innings. Then, up came Junior Caminero with a runner on. After that, it was impossible to drowse off. https://youtu.be/h60gtkCBMBc The numbers on the home run themselves are not very impressive, nor was the timing particularly special. Caminero just dinked the foul pole; Statcast indicates that it would have only been a home run in Houston, New York, and, indeed, Tampa. Speaking purely in homer quality, it paled in comparison to his teammate Yandy Díaz's next-inning dagger. But absent the aesthetic appeal of a no-doubter, or the narrative sway of a game-winner, what made Caminero's home run incredible was Junior Caminero.

item.title: Ghostmashers
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: This time of year, you can count on hearing Ray Parker Jr's "Ghostbusters" quite a bit. Sure, it's still appropriate, and so is the movie, but what it really needs is a mashup with eleven other songs from the 1980s. Yes, twelve songs, and if you don't recognize them all, there's a list at the YouTube page. Bill McClintock revealed this mashup in honor of Halloween. Some of the songs are what you'd normally think of as Halloween songs, but most of them are just dance hits that you know by heart. So you may as well get up and dance to them now!

item.title: I Have a New Cat!
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: This is Toast. I'm sure it's short for Burnt Toast. He's a 6-year-old Russian Blue, and is twice the size of my other cats. That coloring makes him hard to find and he seems to appear out of nowhere. He's a real sweetie.Back in the summer, Dr. Dolittle lost her older orange cat Bread to cancer. It was a very difficult time, and she ended up euthanizing him herself.But what about his companion, Toast? The doctor didn't want to get another cat, and her husband was working in Indiana at the time. She didn't want the cat to be lonely, and besides, they were going to be out of the country for a month this fall. Would I take Toast? Sure! So she brought Toast, and stayed a few days with him. She ended up staying with me four days out of every seven for the next two months, only going home to work. Dr. Engineer joined her here two days a week. Dr. Dolittle really doesn't like living alone. Then her husband got laid off and they are now off in Nepal for a month. So Toast lost his cat buddy, his family, and his home. But he gained his heart's desire, the ability to go outside. My cats hated him from the start- after all, he's strange, huge, and hard to see. But Toast is eager to make friends, and after about three months, they are making progress. Marshmallow has decided he's no threat and just ignores him now. Tommy is okay and will let Toast follow him around, and only hisses when he gets too forward. Sundae still growls at him, but is no longer terrified (she stayed outside for a month when he first came). I've even caught a few nose boops between Toast and Tommy and Marshmallow.Toast has learned how to communicate with me, and goes in and out all day. I think he's testing my limits. Now that it's cold, I make the cats all stay in at night. The other three cats sleep with me at night, but if Sundae is outside, Toast will be on my window table behind the bed when I nap. We are making progress.

item.title: I warned you, now it's happening
item.author: 1axbsa2etu6nm1aaz2l4sb0dn2ltwg3vbhwlwj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: The start of early voting is normally a time for civic celebration. For Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, it was an opportunity to make a threat.Standing beside a Bible and a framed photograph of Donald Trump, Reitz recorded a video promising there would be no “crooked local election administrators.” They “have a duty to prevent illegal voting,” he said, “and I’m here to make sure they do their job.”Then he got to the point: “If you violate federal election law, I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”Reitz did not cite a single example of election malfeasance. Nor did he offer any evidence of fraud.But deterring bad actors wasn’t his real goal. His message was aimed squarely at the county clerks and poll workers who run our elections. And, of course, he was playing to an audience of one in the White House.

item.title: When Tarzan Became an Old Man
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: We are used to a young and virile Tarzan swooping off to the jungle with Jane and assuming they lived happily ever after. But old age creeps up on all of us if we're lucky. It's possible that Tarzan was a lot older than Jane, or maybe she just held up better over time. This skit was aired in 1962 on . Carol Burnett plays Jane and introduces her Tarzan yell, which she brought back every once in a while on. Jack Benny, as always, was the butt of the joke. His very appearance was the joke, and Burnett got all the good lines. (Thanks, WTM!)

item.title: Troma Tuesday: Mother’s Day
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are horror movies about families. There are horror movies about killers. And then there are Troma movies, where the family might be insane, the killers might be wearing homemade costumes, and the entire production seems to have been created by people who looked at good taste and decided it was getting in the way. is a perfect example.Released in 1980 and produced by Troma Entertainment, is a nasty, strange and frequently hilarious piece of exploitation horror that takes the concept of the loving family and throws it directly into a wood chipper. It follows three friends who head into the woods for a reunion and quickly discover that the area is occupied by a deeply disturbed family consisting of Mother and her two sons, Ike and Addley.And these aren’t exactly the kind of people you invite over for Thanksgiving.Mother is the centerpiece of the entire nightmare. She is controlling, violent and completely devoted to raising her sons according to her own horrifying definition of family values. Ike and Addley are essentially grown-up children who have somehow managed to turn their mother’s terrible parenting into a full-time lifestyle.The setup is classic exploitation cinema: three women venture into an isolated area, encounter a strange family and realize far too late that they are in serious trouble.But isn’t content to simply be a straightforward slasher.That’s where Troma comes in.The movie constantly bounces between horror, black comedy, absurdity and outright nastiness. One moment you’re watching a genuinely uncomfortable sequence, and the next you’re wondering whether the filmmakers have intentionally made the entire thing ridiculous.The answer is probably yes.Troma has always understood that there is a very specific audience for movies that don’t know when to stop. is practically a declaration of war against restraint.The production is undeniably low budget, but that works in its favor more often than not. The movie has the grimy, homemade appearance that makes exploitation films from this era so much fun. The woods look genuinely isolated, the interiors feel unpleasant and the whole movie has the atmosphere of something you probably shouldn’t have discovered while flipping through late-night television.The characters are exaggerated, but that is exactly what the movie requires.Mother is not a subtle villain. She isn’t sitting around contemplating the psychological consequences of her actions. She’s a monstrous version of the overbearing parent, except her methods of discipline involve things that would probably get a normal parent arrested approximately twelve seconds after the authorities arrived.Ike and Addley aren’t much better.Their relationship with Mother is one of the movie’s more interesting elements because it gives the story a warped sense of family structure. They are violent because they’ve been raised to be violent, but they are also desperate for Mother’s approval.It’s dysfunctional family therapy with considerably more screaming.The three female leads provide the movie with something important: characters you actually want to see survive.Abbey, Jackie and Trina aren’t simply interchangeable victims waiting for the next attack. Their friendship gives the early sections of the movie a sense of normality, which makes the transition into the nightmare more effective.Once the characters realize what they’ve stumbled into, the movie becomes a battle of survival.And that’s when really starts getting nasty.The violence is deliberately excessive, but the movie’s most memorable moments often come from the combination of horror and absurdity rather than the gore itself. Troma understands that sometimes the best way to make something disturbing is to make it just ridiculous enough that you’re laughing while simultaneously thinking, “This is really messed up.”That balance is difficult.If the movie were played completely straight, some of the material would simply be unpleasant.If it were played entirely for laughs, the tension would disappear.Instead, lives somewhere in between.You never quite know whether you’re supposed to cringe, laugh or wonder how the filmmakers convinced everyone involved to actually make the scene.That’s basically the Troma experience.The movie also has a distinctly early-’80s exploitation sensibility. There is no interest in making the violence tasteful or the villains sympathetic. The film isn’t trying to provide a sophisticated psychological explanation for everything.Sometimes the answer is simply:These people are completely insane.The biggest weakness is that the movie can feel uneven. Some sequences are genuinely effective, while others go so far into camp that the horror almost disappears. The pacing can also feel loose, particularly compared with more polished horror movies from the same period.But polish isn’t really the point.If you want , watch .If you want The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, watch The Texas Chain Saw Massacre.If you want a movie that feels like someone took a chainsaw, a bucket of fake blood, several bad ideas and a deeply inappropriate sense of humor and threw everything into a blender, is considerably closer to what you’re looking for.That’s why the movie has lasted.A lot of horror movies from this era have been forgotten because they were simply trying to imitate whatever was popular at the time. is different. Even when it isn’t particularly good, it is unmistakably itself.The movie also represents something important about Troma’s place in independent cinema. The studio built an audience around filmmakers who didn’t have enormous budgets but were willing to embrace outrageous ideas. The result was a catalog of movies that could be crude, offensive, ridiculous and occasionally surprisingly creative. fits comfortably into that tradition.It definitely isn’t for everyone.But if you’re watching Troma, those probably aren’t the qualities you’re looking for anyway.You’re looking for something that makes you say, “What the hell did I just watch?” accomplishes that goal quite efficiently.The movie takes something universally associated with warmth, family and affection and turns it into an excuse for exploitation horror. The irony is obvious, but the filmmakers never waste much time explaining it.They just keep making things worse.And then somehow even worse. is a filthy little horror movie with a nasty sense of humor, a wonderfully unhinged central family and exactly the kind of low-budget insanity that made Troma famous.It’s a cult movie designed to make you uncomfortable, make you laugh and occasionally make you question your own decision-making for watching it in the first place.And honestly, that’s a pretty good Mother’s Day gift. is crude, violent, ridiculous and completely unafraid of crossing lines. It isn’t polished enough to be considered a classic horror film in the traditional sense, but as a piece of Troma exploitation cinema, it delivers exactly what it promises.

item.title: My obituary for programming
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the of developing code:Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible.If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving.If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real.

item.title: Sometimes A Team Just Wants To Hire A Famous Guy
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The moment general manager Chris Ballard was given Fredo's kiss by the Indianapolis Colts' HR department Monday morning, the rumor mill started to churn up replacements. This is bleak work, but consider that the alternative was analyzing how the Colts managed to lose at home against a previously winless Titans team on Sunday. The first name on that list, per Dan Patrick, was Peyton Manning. It's a perfectly silly, superficial, and absolutely in-play choice for the job: the only person who does insurance commercials more often than Flo from Progressive.That's because Manning is the preeminent former Indianapolis Colt, a quarterback who won a Super Bowl ring for the team and had the best seasons of his Hall of Fame career in that town. It's in play because Manning is an omnipresent medioid who ably plays the affable goober, but is in real life anything but. It's also in play because the Colts are owned by the daughter of the late Jim Irsay, Carlie Irsay-Gordon, an owner who takes notes on the sidelines in a constant quest to avoid just being seen as another fail-offspring in a league that's lousy with them. After the team's final loss of last season, she asked Ballard if he believed he still had "his juju." Given that he got canned with a career record in the job of 72-82-1 and the Colts haven't reached the playoffs since the 2020 season, it puts a serious strain on the concept of "juju."Somewhere in that notebook, at some point during Sunday's grim and lifeless 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans, for god's sake, Irsay-Gordon presumably wrote "this juju sucks," if not in so many words then decisively enough to punch Ballard's ticket. item.title: A Tiny 24 FPS E-Ink Game Boy Emulator
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: This is really impressive: a software engineer got a Game Boy emulator running at 30 fps on a tiny e-ink screen.If you’re familiar with e-paper, you know that they normally refresh much slower (2-3 times a second), not nearly quick enough to play even a simple video game. This guy wrote his own display driver that got the refresh rate up to 30 times per second. From the transcript of the video explaining how e-paper works and how he hacked the display to make it play games:Unlike conventional displays like LCD or OLED, ePaper stores its image physically using charged black and white pigment particles. By changing the electric field, the display moves the pigments towards or away from the surface, which in the end gives us black- or white-looking pixel. And usually a sequence of several electrical pulses called a waveform is needed to move the pigment back and forth, before finally driving it towards the new image. This helps produce a clean result without leaving too much of the previous image behind. But this takes a lot of time.
