item.title: World’s Most Normal Goalie: “The Past Is Dead, There’s Nothing For You There”
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: When last we checked in with Devin Cooley, he was serving as the backup goaltender for one of the worst teams in the league—I mean, downright putrid, couldn't-pay-me-to-watch bad. Not a lot has changed about the Calgary Flames in 11 months. They have two wins so far, second-fewest in the NHL. They have allowed 37 goals, second-most in the league. They're sporting a goal differential of minus-20 in just eight games played, which means that if you attend a Flames game, you should expect to see them lose by multiple goals. In practice they have lost multiple games by four, and multiple games by five.It takes a type to thrive in that environment, and Cooley might be that type. All goalies are strange—they are under constant, ego-deforming pressure, and must spend an unhelpful amount of time alone in their own minds—but Cooley is rare in being able to describe his specific flavor of strange. In that interview last year, he displayed a mindset that, while nihilist on its face, is probably pretty healthy in its ability to compartmentalize each save, each game, and wall it off from the saves and games he has yet to face. "Nothing matters," he said, "nobody cares, we're all going to die."So what would the Flames' poor 2026 start do for Cooley's mood? Well, ah, at least his bunny Tito seems in good spirits. Good for Tito. He's the only living being who can attend a Flames game and not suffer psychic damage.

item.title: How Did A Famous, Lying UFC Vet Get Shot Conducting Shadowy Paramilitary Operations In The Congo?
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: On Oct. 9, the reported that UFC veteran Tim Kennedy was recovering in the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center after he'd been shot three times while conducting a deadly, murkily defined operation with Erik Prince's private military group, in the remote highlands of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwandan-backed rebel group M23. The constellation of proper nouns in that sentence is staggering, and lights the way to understanding the strange, idiosyncratic state of affairs in one of the most mineral-rich areas of the planet. I am going to walk you through this story, proper noun by proper noun (out of order), in hopes of untangling the messy web.Democratic Republic of CongoA few billion years ago, the large-scale geologic province known as the Congo Craton formed. Cratons are geologic provinces that have survived the endless churn of tectonic activity that recycles most of the Earth's crust, meaning they contain some of the most ancient rocks on the planet. In central Africa, the Congo Craton is overlaid by the massive and comparatively young Congo Basin, a sedimentary complex that contains the largest deposit of cobalt in the world, in addition to huge amounts of copper, gold, tantalum, and other valuable minerals.

item.title: Tiny Flame Of Joy Extinguished In Sacramento
item.author: Giri Nathan
item.content:encoded: Where the Sacramento Kings are concerned, all "joy" is relative. But this team, which projects to be among the NBA's worst, enjoyed one charming preseason storyline: the apparent revival of Ben Simmons as an actual rotation player. The basketball gods have chosen to deprive them and their fans of even this meager comfort. ESPN's Shams Charania reported on Sunday that Simmons tore his right Achilles tendon during a Kings practice, ending his season before it really began.Simmons, a former All-NBA selection, went completely unsigned during the 2025-26 season. He deliberately distanced himself from basketball during that time, not even watching a game until the playoffs. That distance allowed the 30-year-old to pursue a maritime passion—sport fishing—and also allowed him to rebuild himself into a player good enough to sign the veteran minimum for a team projected by ESPN to win 21.7 games."I didn't touch a ball for the whole year," Simmons told reporters at Kings media day. "I didn't watch basketball. I just focused on getting my body right and my mind right." Multiple back surgeries had siphoned away his former athleticism. But Simmons observed a "night and day" difference in his mental health, after allowing his back to heal in his year off; affirmed his love of the sport; and, when asked if he could get back to his old self, said: "He's there. He woke up."

item.title: Hyperland, a Prescient 1990 TV Show by Douglas Adams
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I’d never heard of this before: in 1990, the BBC aired a program created by and starring Douglas Adams called Hyperland. It begins with a frustrated Adams throwing his TV out (too linear, too non-interactive) and Tom Baker (from Doctor Who) popping up as an intelligent interactive agent that promises to “do your every slightest bidding, to fetch and carry for you, to work tirelessly and selflessly on your behalf, always ready, always willing, no job too small or too menial”.Circumventing the limitations of ‘linear’ broadcast TV, the 50-minute programme imagines a new world in which an AI software ‘agent’ - brought to life here by Doctor Who favourite Tom Baker - helps the user (played by Adams) to find and access material of interest in a global world of hyperlinked information - text, images, audio and video. Pop-up ‘micons’ (moving icons) conveniently link to interviews with leading technologists of the era (among them Ted Nelson, Robert Winter, Robert Abel, Kristina Hooper, Fabrice Forin and Steve Gano).Some of this stuff has dated badly - few visions of the future get everything right! - but the programme is nevertheless of considerable historical importance.Incredibly, at about the time Hyperland was being broadcast, a young CERN computer scientist by the name of Tim Berners-Lee was beavering away on URLs and HTTP, the foundations of what would become the World Wide Web.Even Adams, who foresaw so much, didn’t anticipate the impact the Web - and the Internet that conveys its data globally - would have on civilisation. Needless to say, the enticing infoworld envisaged in Hyperland was a public-service one of education, art, literature (including nods to Adams’ own works!) and entertainment. There’s no advertising, hacking, cybercrime, information theft, social-media addicts, unaccountable corporate domination or drug-like dependence on the smartphones that Adams himself predicted. And Tom Baker’s enthusiastic agent isn’t forever popping up to try and sell you something…I’m imagining what 16-year-old Jason would have made of this (or HyperCard or hypertext had he had any clue that they existed until 4-5 years later) — his brain probably would have exploded.

item.title: Rolling Snakes Reinvent The Wheel
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: For eons, roly-polies have rightfully dominated the rolling space, at least in our imagination. The crustaceans' astonishing ability to transform from a legged arthropod into a perfect sphere, a behavior called volvation, earned the bugs their nickname. But the bugs are far from the only rollers in the animal kingdom. Pangolins, hedgehogs, echidnas, and armadillos do it too, curling up their bodies into defensive balls. So does the Venezuelan pebble toad, which tucks in its head and tumbles down slopes to escape tarantulas. The Mount Lyell salamander rolls too, coiling itself into a wheel and bouncing down steep rocks. None of these animals become quite as Platonic a sphere as the roly-poly, but they do well enough.But becoming a ball is not the only way to roll. The dwarf reed snake has found another way to roll away from danger, not by becoming a ball but by becoming something like a hoop. This peculiar motion, the mechanics of which are analyzed in a new paper in raises an important question: What is more sinister, a snake slithering in the grass or a snake rolling itself like a possessed wheel?

item.title: Judge Rebukes Trump DOJ for Pushing Her to Recuse
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Trump Calls Judge ‘Crazed Lunatic’Over the past week, the East Potomac Park case has morphed from another of President Trump’s personalist projects in D.C. to a burgeoning confrontation between the executive and judicial branches.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had, by her own admission, bent over backwards to accommodate the Trump administration as it defended its supposedly nascent plan to remake a popular park in the heart of monumental D.C.But then — in violation of her orders that the administration provide advanced notice and a chance for the court to intervene before undertaking any major projects in the park — the National Park Service removed hundreds of trees from the park’s golf course after providing scant notice just before 5:00 p.m. ET on a Friday before a holiday weekend.That led to a fiery hearing in front of Reyes on Columbus Day in which she deplored the conduct of the administration and its DOJ attorneys. The hearing culminated with Reyes temporarily blocking any more tree removals at the park.In the kind of self-defeating move that’s become common in cases where Trump has taken a close personal interest, the Trump DOJ responded to the courtroom woodshedding with a defiant motion on Friday evening calling on Judge Reyes to step aside from the case.The motion to disqualify was over the top, accusing her of “histrionics,” “bias,” “disdain,” “open hostility,” and “animosity” toward the Trump administration in this and other cases.The motion was signed by a single attorney: Stanley E. Woodward, Jr., the No. 3 official at DOJ.Judge Reyes last night denied the motion to disqualify herself but not before eviscerating the Justice Department again: “That is a serious charge. The Court answers it. With the record.”With that prelude, Judge Reyes spooled out pages of transcripts from prior proceedings in the case that rebutted the administration’s claims against her, before concluding:It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion. But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record. By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal.But things didn’t stop there.Trump announced over the weekend that he plans to begin work on remaking the park on Nov. 15, closing it for 15 months. So much for Trump’s plans being nascent, as the administration had insisted for months. Judge Reyes took judicial notice of Trump’s post on Sunday and asked if it changed the administration’s prior position in the case:The Court ORDERS that the Government notify it, by 8:00 p.m. today, whether it continues to take the position that it took in its October 16, 2026, filing, that, “there is no final agency action” and that “at most [] the President has given preliminary thought to” the plan to rebuild East Potomac Golf Course.In its response — signed again only by Associate Attorney General Woodward — the administration insisted nothing had changed.Then came this morning’s pre-dawn tirade from President Trump in which he called Judge Reyes a “crazed lunatic.”Another hearing in the case is underway this morning on whether to issue a preliminary injunction blocking the administration’s plan. In her Sunday order, Reyes upped the ante by requiring Woodward and Deputy Assistant Attorney General Robert N. Stander to appear in person at today’s hearing.We Can Afford to Have Nice ThingsUntil the open clash between Trump and Judge Reyes, I’d hesitated to cover the East Potomac Park case for a national audience because in some ways it’s a parochial D.C. issue and not of the same import as, say, the demolition of the East Wing of the White House, the blight of the Trump Triumphal Arch, the renamings of the Kennedy Center and the Institute of Peace, or the unspeakable painting of the intricate exterior of the grand Eisenhower Executive Office Building.But there’s more going on here than a threat to one public golf course.For those not familiar, it should be noted that while the public golf course within the historic park is at the center of the dispute, the identity, public use, and access to the park as a whole is at stake. The park features a heavily used paved waterfront loop for walkers, runners, and cyclists. It has a playground and picnic area. People fish, enjoy the views of the D.C. core and northern Virginia, and watch planes taking off and landing from DCA.The park was created for the public by Congress in the late 19th century and then was built using fill on the tidal mud flats of the Potomac. The low-cost golf course, like two other public courses in D.C. on National Park Service land, has always catered to a broad clientele, trying to keep the sport accessible.What makes this a national story beyond the clash with Judge Reyes is that the narrowing of public spaces is happening in parallel with the shrinkage of civic life under Trump. The concern is that Trump’s plan would make the golf course more exclusive and less accessible. It would alter the public nature of the park as it has existed for more than 100 years.Let me join the chorus of reviewers urging you to go see Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything.” It’s among the smartest documentaries I’ve ever seen.I came to it unfamiliar with Fielder’s previous work and with only passing Wikipedia-level familiarity with the Theranos scandal.If you’re a Theranos obsessive, you may come away disappointed. It’s not a Theranos documentary. It’s a psychological profile of Elizabeth Homes and of her romantic partner Billy Evans. While it may be tempting to make a judgment on Holmes’ culpability in the Theranos scandal based on Fielder’s work — and audiences probably come out of theaters chatting about exactly that — it would be a mistake.The Theranos fraud, while inextricably woven into the documentary, exists separate and apart from it. Trials and depositions and financial filings and good investigative reporting already explore the fraud itself in great detail. This isn’t that. (If you feel the strong need for a villain in the documentary, Billy more than fills that role on his own — even though he had nothing to do with Theranos and didn’t first meet Holmes until after the company’s collapse.)What really sets Fielder’s documentary apart is its acute self-awareness. It grapples openly with the range of challenges that confront documentarians and storytellers: the limits of objectivity, the nature of truth, the intrusive role of the observer, the inevitability of bias, the constraints of narrative forms. I’m barely even getting started. There’s a going on.Fielder inoculates himself against the most obvious criticisms by confronting them as part of the story he’s telling. It gets super meta at times, but it doesn’t lose the thread of the story. I can’t say much more than that without spoiling it for you.If you’re comfortable with uncertainty, bask in nuance, enjoy the challenge of juggling competing explanations, and can tolerate not having everything reduced to a single “answer,” you’ll delight in this artwork.

item.title: Nobody’s Having More Fun Than Sebastian Fundora
item.author: Dave McKenna
item.content:encoded: Call it a buzzer beating. The reigning WBC super welterweight champ and most interesting man in boxing, Sebastian Fundora, delivered as interesting a knockout as memory serves while retaining his title Saturday night in Las Vegas. Fundora, the tallest 154-pound champ in history (6-foot-5.5 inches) and someone who taunts opponents about the ease with which he makes weight, wounded pesky challenger Ermal Hadribeaj with a vicious assortment of body blows and haymakers to the head as the last seconds of the last round of their brutal and surprisingly competitive 12-round slugfest ticked away. Then, just as the final bell sounded, Fundora landed a lightning-fast kill shot to Hadribeaj’s chin. Referee Thomas Taylor began counting out Hadribeaj, who was sprawled on the canvas, as most onlookers inside the casino arena were wondering what was going on, given that the clock had run out. But, no matter what the title of that ubiquitous '80s and ‘90s sitcom implies, you can no longer actually be saved by the bell in boxing, not even the bell ending the last round. Even though Hadribeaj got to his feet just before getting a 10 count, Taylor ruled he was in no condition to continue. Utilizing the powers vested in him by the so-called Unified Rules of Boxing, a package of uniform edicts which since around the turn of the century have been adopted in Nevada and throughout the U.S. that allows for fights to be stopped even after the final bell under such circumstances, Taylor waved his hands over his head and declared a knockout. (Decorated vets Terence Crawford and Tim Bradley, who sat ringside as working media for the TV broadcast, vented at Taylor after the fight for not letting Hadribeaj go home with a decision loss.)

Donny keeps taking about how Canada should be our 51st state, when in reality he’s already turned the United States into Russia’s 47th province.The Review demands an answer to the question we’re all asking right now: Why is Donny throwing our , Ukraine, to the wolves, while slobbering all over Putin’s ass?President Donald Trump is giving [Putin] aid and comfort.Congress has become a laggard even when it is in session. Now, it’s the political season, so it is inconceivable that midterm campaigns will be suspended to do the nation’s vital national security work. Yet in a properly functioning republic, there would be immediate hearings about this week’s shocking escalation of the Trump–Putin alliance.Look at that: the National Review, actually being on the correct side of an issue. William F. Buckley must be churning in his urn.Meanwhile, has the United States ever had a more useless Secretary of State than Marco Rubio? He’s a feckless idiot. He is absolutely devoid of feck. Can you name one thing that Liddle Marco Big-Shoes has accomplished in his almost two years on the job? No, you cannot. Ask him to take a stand on , and he’ll himself right into that hedge.So when a reporter asked Marco to explain how the Space Nazi’s Starlink satellites came to mysteriously stop functioning properly, leaving Ukraine unable to defend itself, just as Russia was initiating a missile attack, of course his answer was “Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sorta happened.”‘It just sorta happened.’ Stunning answer. It calls to mind Harry S Truman’s famous saying, ‘the buck sorta stops somewhere.’Marco Rubio is useless. He’s absolutely useless. He’s as useless as a marzipan dildo.Oh, please. If Starlink technology is truly that dodgy, that stuff kinda sorta happens, all on its own, then why is the United States using it for its own military operations? That’s the question the worthless scribblers of the corporate-controlled press should be asking Marco.Of course, the Starlink satellites didn’t just mysteriously anything. Someone ordered that shit to happen, and perfectly timed it — either the Space Nazi, or Donny, or the two of them working in cahoots. NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.This should be a huge fucking scandal right now — because once again, Dear Leader is throwing Ukraine to the wolves. Immediately, Congress should hold hearings, demanding testimony under oath from Defense Department and other administration officials about the chain of events that led to restrictions that facilitated Russia’s suspiciously timed attack.And if Marco Rubio can’t come up with a better lie than ‘kinda sorta who even knows,’ then he should resign in disgrace. After that, we all need a palate cleanse — so here comes the part where we all throw our heads back in laughter. Ready?Here’s a perfectly normal billboard that’s currently up in Brownsville, TX, in the district where Republican Eric Flores is running for Congress. The letter says the sign “fraudulently purports to be on behalf of” the Flores campaign. Across the bottom, it says it was paid for by the campaign of Rep. Vicente Gonzalez — the incumbent Democratic lawmaker running for reelection in the battleground district.That’s how toxic Donny has become. No Republican currently running for office wants to be associated with him. Congratulations, Donny. You’re such an utter fucking embarrassment that no one want your fat, waterlogged face on their ads. Oh, look — Jon Ossoff gets to be our Hero of the Day, for the second day in a row.“I have no interest in running for president in 2028, and to be very frank, with just 16 days before the polls close, I want to urge everybody out there to remain focused on the task at hand. The Trump administration is out of control, they’ve lied us into war, they've sent prices skyrocketing...”As soon as any naturally-charismatic politician shows up on the scene, the media immediately starts asking, ‘so ya gonna run for president? ya gonna? ya gonna?’For all we know, Ossoff’s probably lying his incredibly handsome face off. Every elected official thinks they’d be an awesome prez. That’s part of the implicit narcissism that makes anyone run for office in the first place. But Ossoff knows that second he cops to it, it becomes The Big Story, and a huge distraction. So he gives the only correct answer.‘Fuck no, the midterms are right around the corner. That’s the task at hand.’Indeed. The election is 15 days from today. Let’s fucking do this.Well, we’re now all the way down to the bottom of this post, so I guess it’s high time we had us some Daily Claudia.’Tis the season, so here’s a trio of Ms. Spouse documenting the Halloween decorations outside the house of our friends, Nicole and Altin, on October 8, 2021.Have a great Monday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: There’s A Difference Between Honoring A Dead Artist And Exploiting One
item.author: Dave McKenna
item.content:encoded: Another new album of old Eva Cassidy recordings, called , is about to come out. Cassidy, a peerless D.C. songbird, died 30 years ago next month. Her supply of unheard material ran out long ago. Those who legally control Cassidy's songbook transitioned from merely curating her art, as her label still claims to be doing with the latest project, to altering it. gave me the blues.Cassidy's talent was rare and huge, though it took her dying to get the music industry to notice. And the story of her quiet, relatively anonymous life giving way to massive posthumous popularity the world over is equally amazing. When she was alive and singing, Cassidy was unknown outside the D.C. area, where she was born and raised and stayed until the end. She really wasn't a big draw in her hometown, either. She had a small, hardcore group of local fans who loved her for her pitch-perfect voice and multi-genre musical range, and also for being a serene, sweet soul seemingly as oblivious to her own artistic genius as were all the record-label honchos who rejected her when she was knocking on doors looking for a deal. She paid her bills by working at a plant nursery, not by making beautiful music. Cassidy and her band gigged mostly at bars, never at theaters or music halls. She financed her own recordings, including 1996's , the only solo album she lived to see released. But right when that record was about to come out, Cassidy began telling friends she wasn't feeling right, and died from melanoma mere months later. Some Cassidy recordings got into the hands of pop influencers in England in the late 1990s, most notably her cover of "Over the Rainbow," and over the next few years she became a phenomenon throughout Europe and then the world. Another big break came when Team USA's Michelle Kwan skated to Cassidy's version of "Fields of Gold" on the way to a bronze medal during the 2002 Olympics.

item.title: Ta-Nehisi Coates on the Consequence of Donald Trump
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Through a mix of moxie, cynicism, and misanthropy, Trump has made himself into the dominant American of our age. Sometimes a man meets his moment, and Trump met his in the wake of a black presidency and a conservative movement doggedly and patiently pursuing a decades-long counterrevolution. The marriage of Trump’s charisma to a fundamentalist right wing has been bountiful: three Supreme Court justices in four years, the subsequent destruction of national abortion rights, the banishment of affirmative action, the hollowing of the Voting Rights Act.And the genie may not go back in the bottle:But some things can’t be unseen. The example that Trump has set, the scope of what is possible should one embrace the dark powers of the White House, will not dissipate. It turns out that you can deploy secret police onto American streets. You can deport immigrants in defiance of the courts. You can have the Justice Department badger your enemies. And you can become very rich while doing it. And some of the most powerful sectors in America, those who most loudly extol their own love of country, will stand around and watch you do it. Asked why he was making deals during his second term, Trump gave a succinct and chillingly accurate summation: “I found out that nobody cared.” And to the extent that there is a genius to Trump, it is in his apprehension of this reality—so very few people who matter care. When you’re president, they let you do it.

item.title: Jaguars Junction: Week 6

item.content:encoded: Last week, when the Jacksonville Jaguars played the Philadelphia Eagles in London U.K., I devised a typically great "bit." My idea was to write a piece casting Philadelphians as clumsy oafs, juxtaposed with Jacksonvilleans, who would be portrayed as urbane sophisticates. The essay was to start with a dramatic scene of a Philadelphia resident in London, behaving as the proverbial bull in a China shop, demanding: "DUHH ... ME WANT MEAT SANDWICH!" As the poor Pennsylvanian proved himself a rube, the Jacksonville resident, dressed in a rakish Savile Row suit, would shrug apologetically and, with a smattering of cosmopolitan remarks, assure his London host that not all Americans are so painfully uncultured. item.title: Willowbrook State School
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: It wasn't all that long ago that developmentally disabled children, particularly those with intellectual challenges, were hidden away and cared for in institutions. Out of sight, out of mind. The largest such institution in the US was Willowbrook State School in Staten Island, New York. It had a capacity of 4,000, but by 1965, it housed 6,000 residents. By the 1950s, it was clear to the administration that the families of the children living at Willowbrook were not coming to visit, so they could get away with anything. There were unethical medical experiments performed on residents who could neither consent nor complain. After that era, Willowbrook was seriously overcrowded, underfunded, and understaffed. The employees who did their best were forced to take shortcuts because they had too many residents to care for, and other employees were uncaring and abusive. It took a series of exposés to bring attention to the conditions at Willowbrook, and even more horrors were discovered after the school closed.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s fighting style terrifies MAGA
item.content:encoded: Jesse Watters can’t seem to stop admiring Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. The Fox News host loves to talk about how Michigan’s Democratic nominee for the Senate is “in great shape” and how “Abdul . . . beat the machine” — meaning the party establishment’s candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens — in a hard-fought primary. During an interview in August, Watters clearly enjoyed El-Sayed’s jokes and blunt speech, which included calling his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, a “beta,” and asking the host if he was circumcised when Watters tried to corner him on gender-affirming surgery for minors. The next day, Watters made no bones about El-Sayed’s appeal. “I like him,” he said. “I don’t want to like him. I like him for some stupid reason.”But the reason was obvious. The doctor-turned-politician has an aggressive bro style that appeals to someone like Watters. Quick-witted with bulldog energy, El-Sayed never backs down from a fight. But despite Watters’ admiration, Fox News has become obsessed with taking El-Sayed down. It’s not because he’s Muslim, though Republicans are ratcheting up the racism in their efforts to derail his campaign. It’s because he is a model for how Democrats can escape their reputations for being weak and feckless. El-Sayed has a lot going for him. He spent years running public health services in the Detroit area and speaks eloquently and with authority about people’s struggles to afford healthcare, even writing a book about Medicare for All. Most importantly, he’s an excellent communicator who can boil down complex policy ideas into easily digestible concepts without dumbing them down. A video of him explaining to Trump voters why universal healthcare is cheaper than the insurance system went viral for good reason. One can see that, for these voters, it’s likely the first time someone plainly explained how removing executive salaries and profit incentives from healthcare makes it cheaper. Other politicians, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., or Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., are good at explaining progressive policy. But what really seems to scare Republicans about El-Sayed is his political persona as a brawler — and for good reason. Vice President JD Vance learned this last week when he lobbed a strange insult at El-Sayed during a rally in Michigan for Rogers. The Democrat, Vance said, is “a little weasel who should shut his mouth and show a little gratitude.”This is a common and deeply racist attack from Vance, who portrays non-white progressives as undeserving recipients of white people’s largesse — a caricature that has no relation to reality. El-Sayed left a position as an assistant professor at Columbia University to work in public health, where he won awards for his success in protecting children’s health from environmental pollution. During this same period, Vance worked as a venture capitalist who was close with tech billionaire Peter Thiel.El-Sayed resisted the temptation to “well, actually” Vance, and instead hit back by calling the vice president and those around him “carnival barkers” who ““JD Vance called me a little weasel today,” El-Sayed said. “I’m like, ‘No, no, no. What you’re talking about is a Wolverine,'” a reference to the mascot for the University of Michigan, where the Democrat got his undergraduate degree. As Salon’s Sophia Tesfaye recently wrote, El-Sayed has been courting Fox News viewers by appearing on the channel and running endless ads on it, all without softening his left-leaning message. He clearly hopes his bravado will woo some of the network’s audience, just as it won over Watters. For his part, President Donald Trump is worried that El-Sayed is right. He’s been openly complaining at rallies and on Truth Social about how charming the candidate is in his Fox appearances. In early October, Axios reported that the White House contacted the network to complain about El-Sayed’s coverage. Trump was especially miffed at the Democrat’s interview with Martha McCallum, during which the host’s efforts to bait him into saying something that could be spun as “radical” failed. Instead, MacCallum embarrassed herself by defending billionaires hoarding wealth, to which El-Sayed said that he’d rather pay for schools than be so “focused on allowing a billionaire to make another billion.”Since then, it seems that Fox producers got the White House’s message that they have to do something to dirty up El-Sayed. But they’ve learned the hard way that it won’t work to come at him directly, because he ends up dominating interviews and beguiling those who, like Watters, love his commanding and clever style. MacCallum later tried to redeem herself by interviewing progressive activist Corbin Trent and pretending he was a stand-in for El-Sayed.At first glance, Trent performed as Fox producers no doubt hoped he might. He took MacCallum’s bait by defending the Muslim Brotherhood, something that the host could not get El-Sayed to do. The problem, though, is that Trent has no discernible relationship to the candidate. While he has worked for other progressives, including Sanders, I found no evidence that he has even met El-Sayed, much less is qualified to speak for him.This attempt to hobble El-Sayed was revealing; it’s clearly all Fox News has. If the network tries to bring El-Sayed on again to ask him the same questions, they know from experience that he’ll probably just win over even more of their viewers. This isn’t idle speculation. MS NOW recently conducted a focus group with regretful Trump voters in Michigan and found that five out of the six are voting for El-Sayed. Republicans should be worried about the young male demographic in particular. Trump won male voters under 30 by a narrow margin in 2024, but they are jumping ship and now strongly favor Democrats.El-Sayed is a compelling model for a new kind of Democrat. Polling by Strength In Numbers/Verasight shows that even Democratic voters take a negative view of the party, but not because they think their leaders are too progressive. “[T]he single most common complaint about their own party is that it is too weak, too cautious, or not fighting hard enough,” writes G. Elliott Morris in an analysis of the poll.The Democratic base wants the party to take a more aggressive stance toward their GOP opponents, which will be key to building a more lasting coalition — especially one that includes younger and more male voters. El-Sayed is doing just that, and it has the right scared.

It’s not just about the fact that the DOJ is losing and we are winning. These voter roll cases were critical to Trump’s ploy to undermine the midterm elections and control who can vote — and we beat him at every turn.But this fight is far from over. We are still waiting to hear from Delaware and Utah, and Hawaii and Idaho are stayed pending the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decision. I suspect this issue will likely land before the Supreme Court in the coming weeks.When that happens, we’ll be the first to let you know.That’s because I founded Democracy Docket for times just like this. When I write to you about the DOJ voter roll cases, I’m not speaking as a commentator. I’m writing to you as someone who knows these cases inside and out.I’m staying up late to record a video, taking time between reviewing legal briefs to write to you, because I believe that we are facing the greatest threat to our democracy we’ve ever seen.Premium memberships also keep our Democracy Docket’s website, social media and podcasts free for everyone.If now is not the time, I understand and thank you for still staying in this fight with me. It means more than you know.Trump’s voter roll scheme was about one thing: making it harder for you to vote and easier for him to cheat. In courtroom after courtroom, judges stopped him. But he isn’t done, and neither are we.I created Democracy Docket for moments like this, and I’m grateful to face it with you.

item.title: Stuart Bogie (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Stuart Bogie, an American clarinetist and saxophonist from Illinois. We previously featured his music along with a chat in 2023. The occasion was the release of his album , two clarinet improvisations over ambient synth tracks provided by James Murphy of LCD Soundsystem. Those pieces came from a morning ritual Bogie began shortly after covid hit. He expanded the ritual in 2024 when he linked up with organist Buck McDaniel. Since 2024, the pair have played regularly and put on annual fall shows called , which have been released as standalone albums. We’re playing two of those variations today, one from 2025 and the other from 2024. This November they’ll be performing them again. A conversation with Stuart follows the streaming links.You’re performing with Korey Richey of LCD Soundsystem and comedian Rory Scovel soon.Korey, Rory, and I have a performance in Denver. We’re going to start workshopping this collaborative improvisational process. We rented a warehouse. The show’s sold out. It’s an exciting collaboration. There’s something so fulfilling about the power of a musical texture. If somebody steps in and just starts illustrating narrative and dramatic and comedic possibilities that exist within it. I can remember – even if the music is campy or corny or something, as soon as somebody joins it with a narrative context, it can become very affecting. Like if you think about cheap horn samples, some of the hardest music I’ve ever heard has like [horn noises]. It sounds so hard, and it’s like a cheap trumpet patch.I love to hear music recontextualized. The more true and honest and heartfelt the music is, the funnier it will be. In the same way where when you watch a great standup comedian do an incredible impersonation, it feels hysterical because there’s a virtuosity to the authenticity.What instruments are Korey and Rory playing?Korey is doing electronics and guitar. I’m doing woodwinds and electronics. Rory is doing vocals, like comedic – theatrical vocals. We’re exploring different technological possibilities. We’re really just starting off. This is a one way ticket we have together.We’re releasing all of these from last year again. I’m thrilled with how they turned out. Fritz Myers tweaked the recording process, put some mics in different places, and the fact that we’ve been working together for a year since the first one – you can really hear all of those things in the music. It’s almost like a little miniseries. Like a television miniseries where one thing happens after the other. Over the course of the week it’s like five symphonic movements, with the penultimate one being this depths-of-serenity one and the last one containing the most speed and virtuosity. There’s one in the center that feels kind of angular and confrontational. They all have different aspects and colors. As in the first series, Buck’s motivic stuff – his recurring themes and his memory for melodic information – is fantastic. It gives everything a strong focus.Fritz Myers, who produces the event, introduced Buck and me. Fritz is my manager, and early in our relationship, he was like what do you want to do? I said I want to find a place where I can play at 9am every day of the week in a public space. I wanted it to be near my kids’ school, so I can drop them off at school and go and play in front of people, but not necessarily people who expect to see me play. He introduced me to Buck McDaniel, who’s the organist and music director at a church not far from where my kids go to school. We connected immediately musically and artistically and as friends. The music immediately began to unfold from the very first chords.That came out of your daily playing on Instagram after covid started.Yes. Also, in my career, I’ve often focused on making one thing and then putting it away and reinventing a whole other thing to do. I go from far extremes one to the other. Before covid, I started looking at art more. I saw this series at the Guggenheim where they show a bunch of works by a particular artist – I saw this series by the sculpture artist Giacometti. I was struck by all the subtlety that emerges when you see someone doing something similar over and over and over again. I went to an exhibit of John Zorn’s sketches, and I thought about his work, how he will exhaustively go through all the little permutations of a subform. It’s beautiful to watch him investigate every corner of these worlds he takes on.I realized that, in my own way, I needed to have a more repetitive process. I needed to go to the same well for water every day. Through doing that, I’ve gotten a whole new understanding of things, something that I thought was just one approach is dozens of approaches. If I use a rhythm in one piece, now I can use that rhythm in a hundred.Last time we spoke, you talked about Eno and Indian classical as influences. Was there other music that influenced the daily series?I have a teacher named W.A. Mathieu. He has a book called that I read for years and then in the pandemic, I started studying with him over Zoom – specifically the harmonic lattice, as he describes it. That went to work on the way I play music and the way I understand music.What did you learn from that?It increased my understanding of the relationship between the harmonic series, pure intonation, pure ratio, harmonies, and the equal temperament system. I learned a way of moving through different modalities, maintaining the same tonality – what he calls dronality. It’s something that I think most people who’ve taken a long listen and worked on this kind of music experience. His way of describing the subtleties and the tendencies in the melodic and harmonic activity really fit me to a T. It really spoke to me, and I gained a deeper understanding of things, I think. I’m still working on it.One day he said to me, “Stuart, there’s no success in this. You’re not going to win music.”He saw me being hard on myself and he tried to take the pressure off. It’s a beautiful practice studying these things.Any artists or records that stuck with you in recent years?Yeah, for sure. I’m always going to back to ‘90s hip-hop. I love all the layering. I love the line of dissonant sound and the looseness of it. I’ve also been working with a looper a lot, so I’m thinking a lot about DJ Premier and El-P and Erick Sermon. Some of my favorites are probably Jeru the Damaja’s The Sun Rises in the East and Gang Starr’s . Those two records are fantastic, I can’t get enough of them. Nas’s records, anything Q-Tip does.Gang Starr wasn’t the first artist I’d thought of as an influence, but Oneohtrix Point Never said their track “Robin Hood Theory” had a huge influence on his looping and sampling.There’s a trial and error in the composition process that is so rigorous – so deeply rigorous that the results are always one of a kind.You can’t plan the beat or the composition in advance.You have to have the sound at your fingertips. Music is so elusive. That’s what’s incredible about it to me, because if I listen to something for an hour, I might love it. If I listen to something for two hours, maybe I’ll stop loving it, or I’ll start to doubt its beauty. Maybe the first time I hear it, it hits me sideways. So how do you preserve your sense of what you’re hearing? It’s incredible, I’m in awe of it.How did you start playing professionally?In high school and college, I had a band with Zak Mastoon (aka Caural) on guitar, the drummer Andrew Kitchen, the bassist Eric Perney, and the saxophonist Colin Stetson. We had a quartet called Transmission, and we would play around Evanston, IL (1990-1994) then Ann Arbor and Detroit (1994-1998) and San Francisco (1999-2000s). We made it all the way to the Knitting Factory in New York, which was a new music Mecca for us. It was a dream come true to play there.Then I moved to San Francisco, and then Chicago for about six months, and then I moved to New York in 2000. After moving here, I joined a band called Antibalas and I fell in love with the music of Fela Kuti. And I learned to play the saxophone, in order to play that music. The first sound I went for was an afrobeat sound. I bought one of Colin’s old alto saxophones. He stayed in San Francisco. (When I was there, there was no point in me playing a saxophone.) I was working a job in New York, and I got laid off, and I had some time on my hands. So I started learning saxophone. And then I joined Antibalas through a mentor of mine named Michael Herbst, who was an early member of the group. The band was wonderful. They handed me a tenor saxophone and said, “Play this.” I got right to work. For the first time in my life I found I had an aptitude for a certain musical style.You hadn’t experienced that before?No, I had always struggled. I couldn’t play jazz, I couldn’t play blues. I wasn’t that good at classical music. I had gotten through musical school and everything, but one of the things I learned in music school was that I’m not good at playing other people’s music. But I hadn’t played Fela’s music yet. When I found Fela’s music, for the first time in my life I felt aligned. He’s an incredible figure.A few years ago, I went to Lagos and visited the shrine. I performed there with some of my friends from the Antibalas world. The singer Amayo brought us there. He’s the old singer from Antibalas.The last question, which is usually the first question, is what’s your earliest memory of music?A lot of ideas I would feel would come out in little songs that I would sing to myself. I remember picking out a Rush record from the department store because it had a doggy on it. I was a little kid and I was like, “Ooh, doggy on the record.” So I wanted that.The most interesting early memory of music I had was being captivated by a song called “Jam On It” by a band called Newcleus. It planted the seeds for the sort of rhythmic interplay – it set me up to love electric Miles, funk music, electro, hip-hop. It’s an incredible song. I listen to today and get so fired up when I hear it. I’m still chasing the dreams that this song gave me as a little boy. I remember in my school one of the breaking crews had a strobe light and their shadows were cast on the wall. They were doing these fantastic dance moves. I was eight years old, they were all 12 and 13, dealing with the dance floor in a beautiful way. It thrilled me. Also in that song there was a vocoder (I think), and I loved that. I love the robot sounds.

item.title: Powers Jostle Over Oil Prices and US Midterms
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Today’s world would be a fascinating object of study if one weren’t also living in it. The price of energy isn’t the cause of Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity. But for months it’s been driving it to new depths. The price of oil plateaued in early October, which seemed to blunt some of Democrats’ electoral momentum. On Friday though it jumped up again, with the Brent Crude price hitting $110 a barrel, the highest since May. That was the worst of all possible worlds for Trump and that clearly played a key role in his decision to waive sanctions against Russia. Reuters reports that the prospect of greater supply from Russia knocked oil off those highs in early Monday trading in Asia. That was clearly the main goal of that waiver. But just in the last hour, reports have come out that Ukraine launched a massive volley of 1,000 drones targeting Russian energy infrastructure.

item.title: Song Battle: Pulp – “Common People” Vs Blur – “Parklife”
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Two songs. Two bands. Two very different snapshots of British life.Pulp’s “Common People” and Blur’s “Parklife” are two of the defining songs of Britpop, but they approach British culture from very different angles.“Common People” is sharp, bitter and intensely personal. Jarvis Cocker takes a story about class, privilege and someone wanting to experience life like an ordinary person and turns it into one of the great pieces of British pop storytelling.“Parklife” is more observational. Damon Albarn and Phil Daniels create a bizarre collection of everyday British characters, while Blur turn parks, joggers, queueing, working life and suburban existence into something simultaneously ridiculous and strangely affectionate.One tells you exactly what it thinks of class tourism.The other watches Britain being weird and says, “Yeah, that’s pretty much us.”Both became defining Britpop songs.Both are nearly impossible to separate from 1990s British culture.Song Profile: “Common People”Released in 1995 on Pulp’s , “Common People” was the song that transformed Pulp from an acclaimed alternative band into one of Britpop’s biggest acts.Jarvis Cocker describes an encounter with a wealthy woman who expresses a desire to live like “common people.” Cocker immediately recognizes the fundamental problem with that fantasy: for someone with money and privilege, poverty can be experienced as an adventure and then abandoned whenever it becomes uncomfortable.That idea gives the song its bite.Musically, Pulp build the track gradually. It starts with a relatively restrained keyboard-driven arrangement before the guitars, drums and bass gradually turn the song into a massive crescendo.His delivery is conversational, sarcastic and theatrical. He isn’t simply singing the story. He’s practically acting it out.By the final stretch, the song has transformed from an observational story into an enormous release of frustration.It is catchy enough for a stadium.It is specific enough to feel like a short story.And it is angry enough to make the entire thing feel dangerous.Blur released “Parklife” in 1994 as the title track of their third album, and it became one of the defining songs of the Britpop explosion.Where “Common People” focuses on one particular social encounter, “Parklife” throws a camera onto everyday British life and starts filming.The song moves through a series of observations about ordinary existence, with Damon Albarn providing the verses and actor Phil Daniels delivering the unforgettable spoken-word sections.Daniels’ voice is absolutely central to the song.He doesn’t sing in the traditional sense.He sounds like someone who has spent years sitting on a park bench judging everyone who walks past.Musically, Blur keep things relatively simple. The bass and guitar provide a bouncy, almost jaunty foundation while the song’s arrangement constantly reinforces its playful British character.“Parklife” is satire, but it’s not necessarily cruel.It feels like Blur are laughing at Britain while also clearly enjoying being part of it.“Common People” is an extraordinarily well-constructed song.It begins with a story, establishes its central conflict, gradually increases the musical intensity and then explodes into the chorus.The arrangement mirrors the emotional progression of the story.“Parklife” is more fragmented by design. It works as a collection of observations rather than one continuous narrative.That’s part of its charm, but “Common People” has a more complete arc.It feels like a short story set to music.Pulp takes the first round.This is a battle between two completely different approaches.Damon Albarn has a pleasant, understated voice that fits Blur’s observational style perfectly.But Jarvis Cocker is operating on another level.His voice is theatrical without becoming ridiculous, sarcastic without losing the melody and emotional without becoming sentimental.Then there’s the way he gradually increases the intensity as the song progresses.By the final section, he’s practically delivering a monologue at full volume.Jarvis Cocker wins this one comfortably.This is arguably the most important category in the entire battle.“Parklife” is packed with memorable observations and amusing British character sketches.But “Common People” has a central idea that gives every line a purpose.The song isn’t simply making fun of someone.It takes the idea of treating poverty as a lifestyle choice and tears it apart.There is humor, but there is also genuine anger underneath it.Pulp delivers the sharper piece of writing.Round 4: Guitar & Instrumentation“Common People” has a great guitar sound, particularly as the arrangement builds toward its huge final sections.But Blur have an advantage here.“Parklife” is full of little instrumental details that give the song its personality. Graham Coxon’s guitar work, Alex James’s bass and Dave Rowntree’s drumming create a wonderfully tight foundation.The instrumental arrangement is deceptively simple.Everything is exactly where it needs to be.Blur gets the point for creating the more distinctive instrumental package.Now we’re getting into dangerous territory.That one word is practically a cultural institution.Phil Daniels shouts it, the band responds, and suddenly everyone in the room knows what they’re supposed to do.But “Common People” has a monster chorus too.Once that guitar kicks in and Cocker delivers the central refrain, the song becomes enormous.Both are spectacular live.But “Parklife” has the advantage of being almost impossible not to yell.Blur takes the chorus round.“Parklife” is energetic in a completely different way.It’s bouncy, playful and constantly moving.“Common People” starts relatively quietly and then keeps getting bigger until it becomes almost overwhelming.That buildup is the difference.By the end of “Common People,” the song sounds like it has escaped the studio.The guitars are louder, the drums are pounding and Cocker is delivering the final sections with barely contained fury.Pulp wins on sheer escalation.Round 7: Character & PersonalityThis is where “Parklife” is incredibly difficult to beat.The song has characters everywhere.The narrator, the people in the park, the strange observations, the spoken-word delivery from Phil Daniels—it all creates a distinctly British universe.“Common People” has one central character and one narrator.“Parklife” feels like an entire neighborhood.You can practically see the people Blur are describing.Both songs became defining Britpop moments.“Parklife” helped establish Blur as one of Britain’s biggest bands and became almost inseparable from the image of Britpop itself.“Common People” had an equally enormous impact, but its cultural life arguably went beyond Britpop.It became a permanent reference point for discussions of class, British identity and 1990s music.It also transformed Pulp’s profile almost overnight.Pulp gets the edge because the song’s central idea has remained culturally relevant far beyond the Britpop era.Both songs are remarkably durable.“Parklife” is one of those tracks that can come on almost anywhere and immediately change the atmosphere.And Phil Daniels makes it impossible to confuse with anything else.“Common People” is also endlessly replayable, but its emotional intensity makes it a slightly different experience.Sometimes you want to listen closely.Sometimes you just want something fun.That’s where Blur have the advantage.Blur wins on effortless replayability.Round 10: Defining BritpopIf you had to explain Britpop to someone who had never heard it, these two songs would be nearly perfect examples.“Parklife” captures the playful, observational, distinctly British side of the movement.“Common People” captures its sharper, more socially conscious side.Blur made British everyday life sound amusing.Pulp made British class differences sound absurd.But which one better represents the movement as a whole?“Parklife” probably has the broader Britpop identity.Blur takes the final regular round.Round 11: The Tiebreaker — Which Is the Better Song?Forget which song better represents Britpop.Forget the cultural significance.Which is simply the better song?This is where “Common People” pulls ahead.“Parklife” is brilliantly constructed and almost impossibly distinctive. Its spoken-word sections, bouncy arrangement and unforgettable chorus make it one of the most recognizable songs of the 1990s.But “Common People” has more emotional weight.It tells a complete story.It has a clear point of view.It builds musically from beginning to end.And Jarvis Cocker gives the performance an intensity that makes the final section feel like a genuine release rather than simply another chorus.“Parklife” makes you smile.“Common People” makes you sing, laugh, think and eventually scream along with it.That combination is incredibly difficult to beat.Pulp wins the tiebreaker and the battle.The Winner: “Common People”Pulp takes the battle, but Blur made them go the distance.“Parklife” is one of the great character pieces in British pop. It captures an entire world in a few minutes, and Phil Daniels’ performance is so distinctive that the song could never have been mistaken for anyone else’s.But “Common People” has something more.It has a story with a beginning, middle and end. It has social commentary without becoming a lecture. It has humor without losing its anger. And most importantly, it has an enormous musical payoff.Blur looked at Britain and laughed.Pulp looked at Britain and asked why it was like this.“Parklife” is the cheeky one.“Common People” is the heavyweight.The songs are almost perfect opposites, which is exactly why they make such a great battle.“Parklife” captures the colorful absurdity of everyday British life.“Common People” captures the frustration underneath it.And when the final round comes down to which song you would actually want to hear one more time, Pulp has the advantage.Winner: Pulp — “Common People”

item.title: llm-echo 0.5
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account.uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output

item.title: Alina Habba May Have Made a Costly Mistake
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Last week, as part of the emerging “‘Layla’ Coda” moment around President Trump, I flagged this story about a nasty feud between Alina Habba and her erstwhile pal and Trump fixer Ric Grenell. Habba went to the White House with the explosive charge that her now-husband, a Turkish nepo-oligarch named Turhan Mildon, had given $6 million to Grenell for the Kennedy Center, then Trump’s top vanity/legacy project. But Grenell, she claimed, had siphoned the money off, presumably for himself. At the time Grenell was running the Kennedy Center. Mildon first came into the Trump orbit because he had major ties to the Maduro regime and major holdings in Venezuela. So he needed to get juice in Trump world so he didn’t lose his toys when MAGA started dividing up the spoils after the U.S. invasion. But now it seems Habba, now Alina Mildon after her marriage last month, may have bitten off way more than she and Turhan can chew.After making the initial accusation, the Turhans have been talking much less than Grenell. Her story had also shifted around a bit, according to the initial Times report. The $6 million, or possibly $5.6 million, was to be carved out of a $17.6 million check for some other unspecified business deal. But when Habba, or rather her husband’s, lawyers presented the White House with the evidence for this transaction, the source of cash was redacted.

item.title: Good Art Is Worth Waiting For
item.author: Kelsey McKinney
item.content:encoded: This article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.About halfway into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new A24 movie , there is a scene that plays like a memory. Nathan Fielder stands, in the present of the movie, inside a San Diego ocean-front house looking out at the crashing waves, remembering. Then, playing for the viewer: two unidentifiable people in the ocean, frolicking, swimming in the icy cold waves, a blonde woman and a brunette man, both tall, both smiling. The camaraderie between them is undeniable.

item.title: Sweater: Here for It, #
item.author: SRS0=G82P=II=m.ghost.io=bounce+3cffae.7bdc18-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Hi! It's R. Eric Thomas. From the internet?Hi!Oh, everyone in the Northeast went into their cedar chest and pulled out their lil Say Something Sweater this weekend I see! Yes, folks felt a little chill in the air and they said, "lemme go on and hit the people with a Personality Wool right quick."Baby, you better go on with your bad self and your Deliciously Chunky Knit or Cozy Cashmere Cowl Neck. Yes, perhaps it does have the slightest lingering aroma of the dryer sheets you use instead of mothballs to keep your clothes fresh over the winter and yes, it did get a little warm in the sweater in the middle of the day, and yes, tromping all over hither and thither, apple-picking or errand-running or selecting fixtures for your Nancy Meyers-esque kitchen or whatever it is you get up to makes it harder for you to just sit and in this, your Debut Sweater of the Season. But nevertheless, it had to be done. You know she's going to bring it to you every fall!If you're reading this in someplace that's warm, like Los Angeles or Texas or on top of the Burj Khalifa, you are probably not on board with what I'm talking about but I believe that, spiritually, we are aligned. There comes a time in every year when you're like, I've decided to participate in fall. Alert the proper authorities. I might wear cranberry. I might wear canary. I might wear marigold. I might wear olive. You have to be prepared to hold all of those possibilities. I am not in control. The Sweater has an energy all its own. It may not have been the first sweater you wore this year. In fact, it probably wasn't. The Say Something Sweater is the mayor of Knitsburgh. It spends the summer ruling over that little vacuum-sealed bag you keep it in with fairness but firmness. I don't really understand what Soft Power means, but I presume it's about the interior hierarchy of your sweaters and assorted bulky transitional season garments and et cetera.I don't really know why I'm writing so much about Sweaters, to be honest. It's been so long since I wrote this newsletter and now I'm like "hello, yes, I'd like to speak with you about something that probably only exists in my mind."I just love Sweaters so much. And I do feel there's a difference between the Say Something Sweater and the Utility Knits, which I define as a sweater--usually a neutral color--that you just don't think about. It's functional. It's warm. It's for work or for church or for yard work and it's fine but it doesn't insist upon itself.The Say Something Sweater is for when you're fully feeling the fantasy. It might be a bolder color or a more complicated pattern. I feel like Aran sweaters are often Say Something Sweaters, the most famous examples being Billy Crystal's in And Chris Evans's in . Fair Isle Sweaters are often also Say Something Sweaters but they have yet to have a truly groundbreaking cinematic moment as far as I'm concerned. I feel like it's like this: sometimes you're wearing the costume of your life and sometimes you're just dressing. (And I want to add an important caveat: I do not know what I'm talking about I do think I'm correct.)There are Say Something Sweaters for Fall and Say Something Sweaters for Winter and they are the same. Holiday sweaters are a whole different category and I do not, at present, have the capacity to get into it. I appreciate your patience.Anyway, thanks for taking my call. I'll be back next week. I'll probably be talking about something other than Sweaters. But honestly, you never know with me.I do not know what I'm talking about I do think I'm correct,Eric

I recently bought the gorgeous and expensive Plotter, but I don't know how it fits. Or if it fits. I wish I needed it, but I don't think I do. Great, more $$$ down the tubes on a just-in-case.On a positive note, season 4 of The Diplomat is out and I love it. There's something about smart people doing difficult jobs as best they can.

item.title: No Kings Four, fuck yeah
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: More than 3,000 No Kings events took place across the world yesterday, but this time the focus was different. No Kings Four wasn’t about — and voting early, where possible. We need to the shitheads, in numbers great enough that they can’t steal the midterms — because you that they’re going to try like hell to pull some post-election fuckery. In fact, No Kings is already working on their next project — defending the vote.Of course, there crowds, in places such as Denver.But the people I really adore — and want to call out — are the individuals in the far-flung corners of the world who made it a point to let Dear Leader know how just how much he .“Add Isle of Skye, Scotland to the map of No Kings Protests! I can’t wait to vote early when I get home. I imagine the London action was bigger but at least we can say there were two protests in the UK! Indivisible Guide Indivisible Long Island #NoKings#BlueWave”And then there’s , who spends every No Kings Day camped out in front of the US embassy in Talinn, Estonia. Here he was, yesterday.This is how much the entire world loathes you, Donny. Congratulations, you did that!Hey, do you know who can go fuck themselves all the way to Mars? The oligarchs and tech bros, that’s who. They’re terrified of We the People, and they’re doing everything they can to make sure our voices get buried. Yesterday, just as the No Kings protests were ramping up, Meta disabled No Kings’ Instagram account, knocking them completely offline.“We have some breaking news, as we follow No Kings protests nationwide. A spokesperson for No Kings says the main accounts for the coalition on Instagram were frozen, and pulled down, and the administrators lost access to the peak of their national day of action. They say this happened at about 1:30pm eastern. MS NOW is out to Meta for comment. We have not heard back yet.”Meta claimed that the whole thing was just a silly mistake, nobody’s fault, really, ha ha — but it still took them hours to restore the account. “And he came up and he was talking very nicely. And I stood right over here. And I examined his ass.”It’s always something with this corroded old fucksnoot, isn’t it? Remember during the 2024 campaign cycle? Back then, in every single speech, Donny would lapse into some nonsensical reverie about boats and batteries and sharks and what would you do if you fell into the water, would you rather get electrocuted by the shark or eaten by the battery? There was never ever any context for this incoherent rambling, but there it was, in speech after speech.No more. The boats and the sharks have been retired, replaced by Donny eternally examining ass. That must be one hell of a gluteus Jon’s packing back there. Way too much information, President Proctologist. Keep it to yourself.“Now, maybe you saw Donald Trump was in Dalton yesterday, oblivious to the collapse of his presidency. A crowd smaller than this one endured two hours of senile babbling while the price of oil hit its five-month high.”Ossoff excels at knowing exactly where to stick the knife. Back in the Oval Bordello, a ketchup bottle just got hurled against the wall, as Dear Leader hears himself get called senile, and has his crowd size made fun of. Our second hero is Abdul El-Sayed — because he’s so good at saying the things we wish we were smart enough to say.Some MAGA chud named Tommy showed up at one of El-Sayed’s rallies, and was so cocksure of himself that he actually imagined he could disrupt the event by heckling. What happened instead was the Tommy the Chud got his rhetorical ass handed to him. El-Sayed took him apart, just by talking to him, one on one.El-Sayed: “You give me your name, I’ll answer the question.”El-Sayed: “Hi, Tommy. How are you?”El-Sayed: “Are you? Do you know what the Constitution of the United States is?”Tommy: “I have one simple question. Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?”El-Sayed: “Yeah, sure, absolutely. But I want to ask to the question that you’re asking. Why are you asking the question?”Tommy: “Well, because they’re a terrorist group.”El-Sayed: “Okay. No, no, but what are you implying? Do you assume that I wouldn’t?”Tommy: “Because I have not heard you disavow them yet.”El-Sayed: you disavowed them? I haven’t heard youEl-Sayed: “Do you? Great. But here’s the thing about it. You’re asking the question, because implicitly, you’ll assume that I have dual loyalties, right? Right? You assume that somehow I wouldn’t disavow, or that I’ll have some higher order, allegiance, than to the Constitution, correct? Tommy, isn’t that what you imply?”El-Sayed: “Why would you think that about me?”Tommy: “Because I have not yet heard you—”El-Sayed: “No, no, no — why would you actually think that about me?”That’s just the first minute. Please keep watching the entire clip. Spoiler alter: things don’t go too well for Tommy. He gets demolished. Not because El-Sayed insults him back, or makes fun of him, but simply because El-Sayed talks to him like a fellow human being.And, in the end, Tommy the Chud books it the fuck out of there with his tail between his legs.Let’s have us our Daily Claudia, why don’t we.Eight years ago today, we were on a plane to Chicago, on October 18, 2018. You’ve seen shot before.But what you haven’t seen are any of the others from the series.There are more in the set, but I don’t want wear out my welcome, so I’ll stop here.Have a great Sunday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Know before you vote
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: Everyone is rightfully expecting a massive turnout at the polls for the mid-term elections. Appeals to vote are everywhere, but I want to emphasize that people need to study up a little before going to the polls.Embedded above is an excerpt from an informative flyer distributed to voters in Wisconsin with content from the League of Women Voters. The flyer was circulated by Wisconsin Conservation Voters (note "conservation" = environment, not "conservative") in order to call attention not to the candidates but to three proposed state constitutional amendments. One of these amendments is entitled "Freedom to Gather During an Emergency," which sounds like a variation on the basic "freedoms" so treasured by Americans, but it is actually a proposal that would limit or prevent the state from locking down during an lethal virus emergency.I'll not discuss the flyer any further here, because it's a Wisconsin matter, but I would encourage everyone to check various online sources regarding non-candidate proposals on upcoming ballots in your state. (If readers want to alert others re deceptive proposals on other state ballots, feel free to do so in the Comments).
